subject: physics
metaDescription: Learn the foundations of mechanics: displacement, velocity, acceleration, Newton's laws, and how forces shape motion — with free interactive physics lessons.
summary: Mechanics is the branch of physics that describes how objects move and what causes that motion. From a ball rolling down a slope to a planet orbiting the Sun, the same few principles — displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force — govern it all. This page gives you the core ideas, with a free interactive course to practise them.
bodyHtml:
Mechanics is the study of motion and the forces that produce it. Every moving object — a cricket ball, a car braking, a satellite in orbit — follows rules that have been understood since Newton.

The starting point is kinematics: describing motion without asking what causes it. You track three linked quantities: displacement (where something is, relative to a starting point), velocity (how fast displacement changes, with a direction), and acceleration (how fast velocity changes). On a velocity–time graph, the slope gives acceleration and the area under the curve gives displacement.

Dynamics adds the cause: force. Newton's second law, F = ma, says a net force on an object produces acceleration inversely proportional to its mass. The same shove makes a bicycle accelerate more than a car. Newton's first law is the special case: no net force means no change in velocity — things keep doing what they were doing.

You see mechanics every day. When a lift starts upward you feel heavier for a moment — the floor pushes harder to accelerate you. When a bus turns a corner you lean outward — your body tries to continue in a straight line while the bus accelerates sideways beneath you. These aren't new forces; they're just F = ma in a non-inertial frame.

Mechanics also gives you conservation laws. Momentum (mass × velocity) is conserved when no external force acts, which is why a heavy stationary puck barely moves when a light fast one hits it. Energy — kinetic plus potential — is conserved in the absence of friction, letting you trade height for speed and back again.

faqs.q: What is the difference between kinematics and dynamics?
faqs.a: Kinematics describes motion (displacement, velocity, acceleration) without asking about causes. Dynamics asks why motion changes — it brings in force, mass, and Newton's laws.

faqs.q: What does F = ma actually mean?
faqs.a: It means the net force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration. Double the force on the same mass and you double the acceleration. Apply the same force to twice the mass and you get half the acceleration.

faqs.q: Is mechanics still relevant when we have relativity and quantum physics?
faqs.a: Yes — for objects larger than atoms moving much slower than light, Newtonian mechanics is extremely accurate. It's what engineers use to design bridges, cars, aircraft, and spacecraft for most of their flight.

metaDescription: Go deeper into mechanics with calculus: position vectors, differential equations of motion, work-energy theorems, and constrained systems — free interactive course.
summary: Once you know the physical ideas of mechanics, the mathematical formulation lets you solve any motion problem systematically. This page covers the vector calculus approach: writing position as a function of time, differentiating to get velocity and acceleration, and integrating forces to predict trajectories — the language professional physicists and engineers use.
bodyHtml:
The mathematical formulation of mechanics turns physical intuition into precise equations. Instead of saying "the ball speeds up," you write r(t) for position as a vector function of time, differentiate to get velocity v = dr/dt, and differentiate again for acceleration a = dv/dt = d²r/dt².

Newton's second law becomes a differential equation: F = m d²r/dt². Given the forces acting on a body and its initial position and velocity, solving this equation gives the entire future trajectory. For a constant force like gravity near Earth's surface, integrating twice yields the familiar parabolic path: r(t) = r₀ + v₀t + ½gt².

When forces depend on position or velocity — like a spring (−kx) or air resistance (−bv) — the equations become richer. A mass on a spring follows d²x/dt² = −(k/m)x, whose solutions are sines and cosines: simple harmonic motion. The frequency depends only on the ratio k/m, not on how far you pull the mass.

The work–energy theorem emerges naturally from the mathematics. Taking the dot product of F = ma with velocity and integrating with respect to time gives: the work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy (½mv²). For conservative forces like gravity or springs, you can define a potential energy function and write total mechanical energy as a constant of the motion.

Constrained systems — a bead on a wire, a pendulum — introduce reaction forces that do no work. The mathematical treatment uses Lagrange multipliers or generalised coordinates, but at this level the key insight is: constraints change the effective degrees of freedom, and you can often eliminate unknown reaction forces by choosing coordinates that respect the constraints automatically.

faqs.q: Why use vectors in mechanics?
faqs.a: Vectors capture both magnitude and direction in one mathematical object. Instead of tracking x and y separately, a single vector equation F = ma handles all directions at once and works in any coordinate system.

faqs.q: What is a differential equation in mechanics?
faqs.a: It's an equation that relates a function (like position) to its derivatives (velocity, acceleration). Newton's second law F = m d²r/dt² is a second-order differential equation — solve it with initial conditions and you get the complete motion.

faqs.q: How does the work–energy theorem follow from F = ma?
faqs.a: Take the dot product of both sides with velocity v, then integrate over time. The left side becomes work ∫F·dr and the right side becomes the change in ½mv². It's not a separate law — it's a mathematical consequence.

h1: Mechanics numericals, worked step by step
summary: Physics comes alive when you solve problems. This page walks through the numerical approach to mechanics: choosing a coordinate system, drawing free-body diagrams, writing equations, and calculating answers. These are the skills that turn textbook theory into exam confidence and real-world engineering.
bodyHtml:
Solving mechanics problems numerically follows a reliable pattern. First, draw a clear diagram with all forces labelled — weight (mg down), normal reaction (perpendicular to the surface), tension (along the string), friction (opposing motion). The diagram is not optional; it prevents sign errors.

Next, choose a coordinate system. For inclined planes, tilt the axes so one axis runs along the slope. Then the weight splits into two components: mg sinθ down the slope and mg cosθ into the surface. The normal reaction balances mg cosθ, and the net force along the slope is mg sinθ minus friction.

A typical numerical: a 5 kg block on a 30° incline with μ = 0.2. Acceleration? Weight component down slope = 5 × 9.8 × sin 30° = 24.5 N. Normal = 5 × 9.8 × cos 30° = 42.4 N. Friction = 0.2 × 42.4 = 8.5 N. Net force = 24.5 − 8.5 = 16.0 N. a = F/m = 16.0/5 = 3.2 m/s².

Projectile problems split naturally into horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (constant acceleration g = 9.8 m/s² down). The time of flight comes from the vertical motion alone. For a projectile launched at speed u at angle θ, time to peak = u sinθ / g, and total flight time is double that. Range = (u² sin 2θ)/g — maximum at 45°.

Collision problems use conservation of momentum: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂. For elastic collisions, kinetic energy is also conserved, giving a second equation. For perfectly inelastic collisions, the bodies stick together and you only need momentum. In all cases, draw before-and-after diagrams and assign positive directions consistently.

faqs.q: How do I approach an inclined plane problem?
faqs.a: Draw the plane, label the angle θ, draw the block, and split gravity into mg sinθ (along the slope) and mg cosθ (into the slope). The normal force equals mg cosθ. Net force along the slope = mg sinθ − friction. Then use F = ma.

faqs.q: Why does a 45° launch give maximum range?
faqs.a: The range formula is R = (u² sin 2θ)/g. sin 2θ reaches its maximum value of 1 when 2θ = 90°, so θ = 45°. At steeper or shallower angles, sin 2θ is smaller, so the range is shorter.

faqs.q: When do I use conservation of momentum vs conservation of energy?
faqs.a: Momentum is conserved whenever no external force acts (or net external force is zero). Kinetic energy is only conserved in perfectly elastic collisions. In inelastic collisions, some kinetic energy converts to heat or deformation — use momentum conservation alone.

metaDescription: Understand forces and motion: free-body diagrams, balanced and unbalanced forces, friction, and how Newton's laws predict every movement — free interactive course.
summary: Everything that starts, stops, speeds up, slows down, or changes direction does so because of forces. This page explains the relationship between forces and motion — how to identify forces, draw them, add them, and use them to predict what an object will do next. A free interactive course lets you test each idea.
bodyHtml:
A force is a push or a pull — nothing more. When you kick a football, the Earth pulls an apple, or a magnet attracts iron, a force is acting. Forces are vectors: they have both size (newtons) and direction. The net force on an object is the vector sum of all individual forces acting on it.

The tool for untangling forces is the free-body diagram: draw the object as a dot, then draw every force as an arrow pointing in the direction it acts. Weight always points straight down. Normal reaction is perpendicular to the surface. Tension pulls along the string. Friction opposes motion (or attempted motion) along the surface. If the object is in equilibrium — stationary or moving at constant velocity — the arrows must sum to zero in every direction.

When forces are unbalanced, acceleration happens. Newton's second law, a = F_net/m, tells you exactly how much. A net force of 10 N on a 2 kg mass produces 5 m/s². The same 10 N on a 10 kg mass produces only 1 m/s² — mass resists acceleration. This resistance is inertia.

Friction deserves special attention. Static friction (before something slides) is a self-adjusting force: it grows to match the applied push, up to a maximum μ_sN. Once the push exceeds that limit, kinetic friction takes over at μ_kN, which is usually slightly smaller. This is why it's harder to start a heavy box moving than to keep it sliding.

Forces also come in pairs — Newton's third law. If you push on a wall with 50 N, the wall pushes back on you with 50 N. Both forces are equal and opposite, but they act on different objects, so they don't cancel. The wall's push on you can accelerate you backward; your push on the wall might deform it.

faqs.q: What is a free-body diagram?
faqs.a: It's a sketch showing a single object isolated from its surroundings, with all forces acting ON that object drawn as arrows. It's the essential first step in any mechanics problem — if you get the forces right, the equations follow.

faqs.q: Why don't action and reaction forces cancel out?
faqs.a: Because they act on different objects. When you punch a bag, the bag punches your fist back equally hard. The bag's force accelerates your fist backward; your force accelerates the bag forward. They don't cancel because they're not on the same object.

faqs.q: What's the difference between static and kinetic friction?
faqs.a: Static friction stops an object from starting to slide — it adjusts up to its maximum. Kinetic friction acts while the object is already sliding and is usually slightly smaller. That's why you feel a 'breakaway' when a heavy object finally starts moving.

metaDescription: Understand energy: kinetic, potential, work, conservation of energy, and power — the core concepts that unify all of physics, with a free interactive course.
summary: Energy is the currency of physics — it's never created or destroyed, only shifted from one form to another. This page covers kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, the work–energy link, and why conservation of energy is the most powerful problem-solving tool you have.
bodyHtml:
Energy is a scalar quantity measured in joules (J). Unlike force or velocity, it has no direction — just an amount. The most important fact about energy is the law of conservation: in an isolated system, the total energy never changes. It can transform — kinetic to thermal, chemical to electrical — but the sum is constant.

Kinetic energy (KE = ½mv²) is the energy of motion. A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s carries 200 kJ of kinetic energy. Because velocity is squared, doubling the speed quadruples the energy — which is why high-speed crashes are so much more destructive.

Gravitational potential energy (GPE = mgh near Earth's surface) is energy stored by position in a gravitational field. Lift a 1 kg book 2 metres and you've given it about 19.6 J of extra potential energy. Let go and that energy converts smoothly to kinetic energy as it falls — when it hits the ground (at about 6.3 m/s), ½mv² = mgh exactly, minus any air resistance.

Work is the mechanism of energy transfer. When a force F pushes an object through a displacement s, the work done is Fs cosθ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. If the force is perpendicular to the motion (like the normal force on a sliding block), it does zero work. The work–energy theorem says the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/t, measured in watts (J/s). A 60 W light bulb converts 60 J of electrical energy every second. An Olympic weightlifter snatching 150 kg through 2 m in 1 second delivers about 3000 W — fifty light bulbs' worth, for a single explosive moment.

faqs.q: What is the difference between energy and power?
faqs.a: Energy is the capacity to do work, measured in joules. Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or converted, measured in watts (joules per second). A battery stores energy; a motor's power rating tells you how fast it can use that energy.

faqs.q: Is energy really always conserved?
faqs.a: Yes — in a closed system, total energy is constant. It can change form (kinetic → thermal through friction, for example) and it can spread out and become less useful, but the total quantity never changes. This is one of physics' most thoroughly tested laws.

faqs.q: Why is kinetic energy ½mv² and not mv?
faqs.a: It follows from the work–energy theorem. The work done to accelerate an object from rest to speed v is F·s = (ma)·(v²/2a) = ½mv². The squared relationship means energy grows faster than speed — a fact with real consequences for braking distances and crash severity.

metaDescription: How gravity works: Newton's law of gravitation, g vs G, weight, free fall, and why everything falls at the same rate — free interactive physics course.
h1: Gravity, from Newton to everyday life
summary: Gravity is the weakest of the fundamental forces, yet it shapes the universe. Every mass attracts every other mass. This page explains Newton's law of universal gravitation, the difference between g and G, why all objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum, and what weightlessness really means.
bodyHtml:
Newton's law of universal gravitation says every pair of masses attracts with a force F = Gm₁m₂/r², where G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². The force is proportional to each mass and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. Double the distance, and the force drops to one quarter.

Near the Earth's surface, this simplifies enormously. Plug Earth's mass (5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) and radius (6.37 × 10⁶ m) into Gm_E/r_E² and you get 9.8 m/s² — the familiar g. This is the local gravitational field strength, or acceleration of free fall. Every kilogram of mass near Earth's surface experiences a downward force of about 9.8 N.

The crucial distinction: g (lowercase, 9.8 N/kg or m/s²) is the local field strength at a particular location — it varies slightly across Earth's surface. G (uppercase, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹) is the universal constant that appears in the full inverse-square law everywhere in the universe. They're related by g = GM_E/r_E², but they are not the same thing.

Why do a hammer and a feather fall together on the Moon? Gravity pulls harder on the hammer (F = mg is larger), but the hammer also has more inertia — it resists acceleration proportionally. The mass cancels: a = F/m = mg/m = g, the same for both. Remove air resistance and all objects accelerate identically. This equivalence was Galileo's insight and Einstein made it the foundation of general relativity.

Orbital motion is continuous free fall. The International Space Station is pulled by almost the same g we feel (about 90% of surface value), but its sideways speed is so high that Earth curves away beneath it as fast as it falls. The astronauts aren't beyond gravity — they're falling together with their spacecraft, so they feel no contact force. That's weightlessness.
keywords: why do objects fall at same rate

faqs.q: What is the difference between g and G?
faqs.a: g (~9.8 N/kg) is the local gravitational field strength at Earth's surface — it varies slightly by location. G (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²) is the universal gravitational constant, the same everywhere in the universe, which appears in the full inverse-square law.

faqs.q: Why do astronauts feel weightless in orbit?
faqs.a: They are in continuous free fall around Earth together with their spacecraft. There is no contact force pushing on them, so they feel weightless — not because gravity is absent (it's about 90% of surface strength at ISS altitude).

faqs.q: If gravity is so weak, why does it dominate the universe?
faqs.a: Gravity has infinite range and is always attractive — there's no negative mass to cancel it. Over cosmic distances, the electromagnetic forces tend to cancel (positive and negative charges balance out), but gravity just keeps adding up. It's also what curves spacetime in general relativity.

summary: Every number in physics carries a unit and an uncertainty. Dimensional analysis — checking that equations have consistent units — catches mistakes before you calculate. This page covers SI base units, derived units, significant figures, errors, and how to use dimensions as a built-in error checker for any formula.
bodyHtml:
Physics is a quantitative science, and every quantity has dimensions. Length [L], mass [M], time [T], electric current [I], temperature [K], amount of substance [mol], and luminous intensity [cd] are the seven SI base dimensions. Every other physical quantity is a combination of these. Speed is [L]/[T]; force (from F = ma) is [M][L]/[T]²; energy (from ½mv²) is [M][L]²/[T]².

Dimensional analysis is the art of checking equations by comparing dimensions. If you derive a formula for the period of a pendulum and get T = 2π√(g/L), something is wrong — g/L has dimensions [T]⁻², so its square root is [T]⁻¹, not [T]. The correct form T = 2π√(L/g) gives [T] = √([L]/([L]/[T]²)) = [T]. This check takes seconds and catches sign errors, missing square roots, and inverted fractions.

SI units give every dimension a standard measure. Length is the metre (m), defined by the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. Mass is the kilogram (kg). Time is the second (s). Derived units combine these: force is the newton (N = kg·m/s²), energy the joule (J = N·m), power the watt (W = J/s).

No measurement is exact. Significant figures communicate precision: 3.0 m means you're confident to ±0.05 m; 3.00 m means ±0.005 m. When multiplying, the result has as many significant figures as the least precise input. When adding, it's the least precise decimal place that limits. Errors come in two types: systematic (always off in the same direction — a zero error on a balance) and random (scatter around the true value). Random errors decrease with repeated measurements; systematic errors don't.

faqs.q: What is dimensional analysis used for?
faqs.a: It checks whether an equation can possibly be correct by comparing the physical dimensions on both sides. If the dimensions don't match, the equation is definitely wrong. It can also help derive the form of unknown relationships by matching dimensions.

faqs.q: How do I know how many significant figures to use?
faqs.a: In multiplication and division, the result gets as many significant figures as the input with the fewest. In addition and subtraction, the result gets as many decimal places as the input with the fewest decimal places. Never invent precision your measurements don't support.

faqs.q: What's the difference between precision and accuracy?
faqs.a: Precision is how closely repeated measurements agree with each other (low random error). Accuracy is how close the average is to the true value (low systematic error). A measurement can be precise but inaccurate (all shots in a tight group, but off-target).

h1: Vector products — the two ways to multiply vectors
summary: Vectors can be multiplied in two fundamentally different ways. The dot product gives a scalar — it measures how much two vectors align. The cross product gives a vector — it measures the oriented area they span. These operations aren't abstract; they're the mathematics behind work, torque, magnetic force, and angular momentum.
bodyHtml:
There are exactly two ways to multiply two vectors in three dimensions, and they answer different questions.

The dot product (scalar product): a·b = |a||b| cosθ. It's a single number — maximum when the vectors point the same way (cos 0° = 1), zero when they're perpendicular (cos 90° = 0), negative when they point more opposite than together. Computationally, a·b = a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z. Dot products answer the question: how much of one vector lies along another?

In physics, work is the dot product of force and displacement: W = F·s = Fs cosθ. Push a crate horizontally (θ = 0) and all your force does work. Carry it horizontally while supporting its weight vertically (θ = 90°) and you do zero work on the crate, because the force and displacement are perpendicular. Power, too, is a dot product: P = F·v.

The cross product (vector product): a×b = |a||b| sinθ n̂, where n̂ is a unit vector perpendicular to both a and b, following the right-hand rule. The magnitude is the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b — maximum when perpendicular (sin 90° = 1), zero when parallel (sin 0° = 0). Unlike the dot product, a×b = −(b×a); order matters.

Torque is the cross product of position and force: τ = r×F. The torque is perpendicular to both — if you push horizontally on a wrench, the torque points along the bolt's axis. Angular momentum is L = r×p. Magnetic force on a moving charge is F = qv×B — the force is perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field, which is why charged particles spiral in magnetic fields.

faqs.q: When do I use the dot product vs the cross product?
faqs.a: Use the dot product when you want the component of one vector along another (work, power, projection). Use the cross product when you need a vector perpendicular to two given vectors (torque, angular momentum, magnetic force).

faqs.q: What does the cross product magnitude really mean?
faqs.a: Geometrically, |a×b| = |a||b| sinθ is the area of the parallelogram formed by vectors a and b. Physically, for torque τ = r×F, it's the product of the lever arm and the perpendicular component of force — the 'turning effectiveness'.

faqs.q: Why is a×b = −(b×a)?
faqs.a: The cross product is antisymmetric. The right-hand rule gives opposite directions when you swap the order: fingers of right hand curl from a to b, thumb points one way; curl from b to a, thumb points the opposite way. This matters — F×r gives the wrong torque direction.

metaDescription: Understand measurement errors (systematic vs random), absolute and relative error, and relative motion in one and two dimensions — free interactive course.
summary: Physics demands honesty about uncertainty. This page covers how to quantify errors — absolute, relative, and percentage — and how motion looks different from different reference frames. A boat crossing a river, a plane in a crosswind, a passenger walking on a moving train: all are relative motion problems.
bodyHtml:
Every measurement has error, and reporting a number without its uncertainty is incomplete. Absolute error is the raw uncertainty in the units of the measurement: a length of 5.3 ± 0.1 cm means the true value likely lies between 5.2 and 5.4 cm. The ±0.1 is the absolute error. Relative error is the absolute error divided by the measured value: 0.1/5.3 ≈ 0.019, or 1.9%. Percentage error is relative error × 100%.

When you combine measurements, errors propagate. For addition and subtraction, absolute errors add (in quadrature for independent random errors). For multiplication and division, relative errors add. If you measure a rectangle as 5.0 ± 0.1 cm by 3.0 ± 0.1 cm, the area's relative error is roughly 0.1/5.0 + 0.1/3.0 = 5.3%, so area = 15.0 ± 0.8 cm².

Relative motion is the observation that velocity depends on who's measuring. A passenger walking forward at 1 m/s inside a train moving at 30 m/s is moving at 31 m/s relative to the ground — but only 1 m/s relative to the train. The general rule: v_(A relative to C) = v_(A relative to B) + v_(B relative to C). This is Galilean relativity — it works perfectly for everyday speeds.

In two dimensions, relative velocity becomes vector addition. A boat that can row at 5 m/s in still water, crossing a river flowing at 3 m/s, has a resultant velocity found by vector addition. To head straight across, the boat must point partly upstream — the upstream component cancels the flow. The crossing time depends only on the perpendicular component of velocity, not on the downstream drift.

Rain falling vertically at 8 m/s appears to a runner (4 m/s) as slanting in from ahead at √(8² + 4²) = 8.9 m/s at an angle tan⁻¹(4/8) = 26.6° from the vertical. This is why you tilt an umbrella forward when you walk in rain — in your frame, the rain has a horizontal component.

faqs.q: What's the difference between systematic and random errors?
faqs.a: Systematic errors are consistent biases — like a scale that always reads 0.2 kg too high. They affect accuracy. Random errors are unpredictable scatter around the true value — they affect precision. Repeating measurements reduces random error but not systematic error.

faqs.q: How do I add relative velocities in two dimensions?
faqs.a: Use vector addition. Draw each velocity as an arrow, place them tip-to-tail, and the resultant is the arrow from the start of the first to the tip of the last. The magnitude is √(v_x² + v_y²) and the direction is tan⁻¹(v_y/v_x).

faqs.q: Why does a boat take the same time to cross a river regardless of the current?
faqs.a: Because the current is perpendicular to the boat's intended path. The downstream drift adds a sideways component but doesn't affect the forward component of velocity. Time = width / forward speed — the current only determines where you land, not when.

h1: Newton's laws and forces, one by one
summary: Newton's three laws are the foundation of classical mechanics. The first law defines inertia and equilibrium. The second law quantifies how forces cause acceleration. The third law explains why forces always come in pairs. This page walks through all three with worked examples and free-body diagrams.
bodyHtml:
Newton's first law (the law of inertia): an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it. This is not trivial — it overturns the ancient idea that rest is the natural state. A hockey puck sliding on frictionless ice would glide forever at constant speed. In everyday life, friction hides this by bringing things to a stop.

Newton's second law: F_net = ma. The net force on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration. This is the quantitative engine of mechanics. The net force is the vector sum of all individual forces — you must add them as vectors, not just magnitudes. A 2 kg block pulled right with 10 N and left with 4 N has net force 6 N right and accelerates at 3 m/s² right.

Newton's third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A. These forces act on different bodies, so they don't cancel. The Earth pulls you down with your weight mg; you pull the Earth up with exactly the same force — but Earth's enormous mass means its acceleration is negligible.

Common forces to identify in problems: Weight (mg, always vertically down). Normal reaction (perpendicular to the contact surface — it adjusts to whatever value needed, up to the breaking point of the surface). Tension (the pull along a string or rope — same magnitude at both ends for a massless, inextensible string). Friction (parallel to the surface, opposing motion or attempted motion). Spring force (F = −kx, restoring, proportional to extension or compression).

In a typical pulley problem, two masses hang on either side. The heavier one accelerates down, the lighter one up. The tension is the same throughout the string (massless string assumption). Set up F = ma for each mass, solve the simultaneous equations, and both acceleration and tension emerge. The approach is always the same: isolate each body, draw the forces, write the equations.

faqs.q: What does Newton's first law really mean?
faqs.a: It means no force is needed to keep something moving — only to change its motion. Constant velocity is just as 'natural' as being at rest. This broke with Aristotle's idea that rest was the natural state and motion required a continuous cause.

faqs.q: How do I solve pulley problems?
faqs.a: Assume the string is massless and inextensible (same tension throughout, same acceleration magnitude for both masses). Draw a free-body diagram for each mass separately. Write F = ma for each, choosing the direction of motion as positive. Solve the two equations together for acceleration and tension.

faqs.q: Why doesn't the normal force always equal mg?
faqs.a: The normal force is whatever magnitude keeps the object from penetrating the surface. On a flat horizontal surface with no other vertical forces, N = mg. But if you push down or pull up on the object, or if the surface is inclined, N adjusts. It's a constraint force, determined by the geometry, not a fixed formula.

metaDescription: Master static and kinetic friction, centripetal force, banking of roads, and conical pendulums — the forces behind every turn and curve. Free interactive course.
summary: Friction makes walking, driving, and braking possible. Circular motion is acceleration toward the centre at every instant, even at constant speed. This page connects both: friction provides the centripetal force that keeps a car on a curved road. From banked turns to the conical pendulum, every example uses the same F = ma logic.
bodyHtml:
Friction is the force that opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact. Static friction (f_s ≤ μ_s N) prevents surfaces from starting to slide; it's a self-adjusting force that matches the applied push up to its maximum. Kinetic friction (f_k = μ_k N) acts once sliding has started and is typically smaller than the maximum static friction — which is why antilock brakes pulse to keep tyres in the static regime.

Friction does not always oppose motion in the obvious way. When you walk, your foot pushes backward on the ground; static friction from the ground pushes forward on your foot, accelerating you. When a car accelerates, it's friction from the road on the drive wheels that provides the forward force. Without friction, wheels just spin in place.

Uniform circular motion is motion at constant speed around a circle. The speed is constant, but the velocity is not — its direction changes continuously. The acceleration points toward the centre of the circle and has magnitude a_c = v²/r = ω²r. The net force must also point toward the centre: F_c = mv²/r. This centripetal force is not a new type of force — it's provided by tension (a ball on a string), gravity (a satellite), friction (a car cornering), or the normal force (a roller coaster loop).

On a flat, unbanked curve, friction provides the centripetal force: μ_s mg ≥ mv²/r. The maximum safe speed is v_max = √(μ_s g r). On a banked curve (angle θ), the horizontal component of the normal force helps: tanθ = v²/(rg) for the ideal banking angle where no friction is needed. Real roads and railway tracks are banked so that vehicles can take curves at design speed without relying on friction alone.

The conical pendulum — a mass swinging in a horizontal circle at the end of a string — combines tension and circular motion. The vertical component of tension balances weight (T cosθ = mg), and the horizontal component provides centripetal force (T sinθ = mv²/r). Dividing gives tanθ = v²/(rg). The period turns out to depend only on the vertical height of the cone, not on the mass or the string length directly.

faqs.q: Why is static friction usually larger than kinetic friction?
faqs.a: When surfaces are at rest relative to each other, microscopic asperities have time to settle into closer contact, creating stronger bonds. Once sliding starts, the surfaces ride over each other with less intimate contact, reducing the friction force.

faqs.q: Is centripetal force a new type of force?
faqs.a: No — 'centripetal' just means 'toward the centre.' The actual force is always something familiar: tension, gravity, friction, or the normal force. You identify the real force and set its radial component equal to mv²/r.

faqs.q: Why are roads banked on curves?
faqs.a: Banking tilts the normal force so it has a horizontal component pointing toward the centre of the curve. This helps provide the centripetal force, reducing the reliance on friction. At the ideal banking angle for a given speed, no friction is needed at all.

h1: Work, energy, and momentum — mechanics' conservation laws
summary: Energy and momentum are the two great conserved quantities in mechanics. When forces are too complicated to track moment by moment, conservation laws cut through the complexity. This page covers work, the work–energy theorem, potential energy, impulse, momentum conservation, and how to solve collision problems efficiently.
bodyHtml:
Work is the transfer of energy by a force acting through a displacement: W = Fs cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force vector and the displacement vector. A force perpendicular to the motion does zero work — this is why the magnetic force on a moving charge changes its direction but never its speed (and thus never its kinetic energy). Work is measured in joules (J).

The work–energy theorem is a direct consequence of F = ma: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, W_net = ΔKE = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i². This lets you bypass time and acceleration entirely. To find the speed of a sled at the bottom of a frictionless hill, you don't need to solve for acceleration — just set mgh = ½mv², and v = √(2gh).

Conservative forces (gravity, spring force, electrostatic force) have an associated potential energy. The work they do is independent of path and equals the negative change in potential energy. For gravity near Earth's surface, U = mgh. For a spring, U = ½kx². When only conservative forces act, mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved — you can trade kinetic for potential and back without loss.

Momentum (p = mv) is a vector. Impulse (J = F_avg Δt) equals the change in momentum. This is why airbags work: by extending the collision time, they reduce the average force for the same change in momentum. A driver stopping from 15 m/s in 0.05 s (dashboard) experiences 300 times body weight in average force; extending to 0.5 s (airbag) cuts it to 30 times.

In collisions, total momentum is always conserved (no external forces). For elastic collisions, kinetic energy is also conserved — solve momentum and energy equations simultaneously. For perfectly inelastic collisions, the bodies stick together — only momentum conservation is needed. Most real collisions lie between these extremes, described by the coefficient of restitution e = (v_separation)/(v_approach).

faqs.q: When should I use energy vs momentum to solve a problem?
faqs.a: Use energy when you only care about speeds (scalars) and forces are conservative — it avoids dealing with time. Use momentum for collisions and explosions where forces are brief and unknown. For collisions, you often need both: momentum gives one equation, energy (or coefficient of restitution) gives the second.

faqs.q: What is impulse and why does it matter?
faqs.a: Impulse is the product of average force and the time it acts: J = FΔt. It equals the change in momentum. The same momentum change can come from a large force briefly or a small force over a long time — this is why catching an egg with a 'giving' motion prevents it from breaking.

faqs.q: What's the difference between elastic and inelastic collisions?
faqs.a: In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is conserved — the objects bounce apart with no permanent deformation or heating. In an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy is converted to other forms (heat, sound, deformation). A perfectly inelastic collision is one where the objects stick together afterward.

metaDescription: Master vectors: addition, subtraction, resolution into components, unit vectors, and vector applications in force, velocity, and displacement. Free course.
summary: Many physical quantities aren't just a number — they point somewhere. Force, velocity, acceleration, momentum, and electric field are all vectors. This page covers vector addition (triangle and parallelogram laws), resolution into perpendicular components, unit vectors, and why treating direction properly is essential to getting physics right.
bodyHtml:
A scalar has only magnitude: mass (5 kg), temperature (300 K), energy (50 J). A vector has magnitude and direction: displacement (5 m north), velocity (20 m/s at 30° above horizontal), force (10 N downward). Vectors don't add like ordinary numbers — 3 N east plus 4 N north is 5 N at 53° northeast, not 7 N.

Vector addition follows the triangle law: place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first; the resultant goes from the start of the first to the tip of the second. Equivalently, the parallelogram law: complete the parallelogram and the diagonal is the sum. For subtraction, a − b = a + (−b) — reverse the direction of b and add.

The most powerful technique is resolution into components. Choose perpendicular axes (usually x and y), and replace each vector with its projection onto each axis. A vector of magnitude A at angle θ from the x-axis has components A_x = A cosθ, A_y = A sinθ. Once everything is in component form, vector addition becomes ordinary arithmetic: R_x = ΣA_x, R_y = ΣA_y. The resultant magnitude is √(R_x² + R_y²) and direction is tan⁻¹(R_y/R_x).

Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ are dimensionless vectors of length 1 pointing along the x, y, z axes. Any vector can be written as A = A_x î + A_y ĵ + A_z k̂. This notation makes vector algebra compact: the dot product a·b = a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z, and the cross product a×b can be computed as a determinant.

In equilibrium problems, the net force is zero — all force vectors form a closed polygon when placed tip-to-tail. For three coplanar forces in equilibrium, Lami's theorem gives a quick relationship: F₁/sinα = F₂/sinβ = F₃/sinγ, where each angle is opposite its corresponding force in the force triangle.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a scalar and a vector?
faqs.a: A scalar has only magnitude (size), like mass or temperature. A vector has both magnitude and direction, like velocity or force. Adding two scalars is just arithmetic; adding two vectors requires accounting for direction using geometry or components.

faqs.q: Why do we resolve vectors into components?
faqs.a: Components turn vector problems into independent one-dimensional problems along each axis. Forces in the x-direction only affect x-motion, and forces in y only affect y-motion. This decoupling makes complex problems tractable.

faqs.q: What are unit vectors for?
faqs.a: Unit vectors (î, ĵ, k̂) provide a compact way to write any vector as a sum of axis-aligned pieces. They turn vector operations into algebraic ones: dot products become sums of products of components, and cross products become determinants.

h1: Electricity and circuits, from charge to current
summary: Electric circuits move charge to do work — lighting bulbs, driving motors, powering processors. This page covers the core ideas: charge, current, voltage, and resistance; Ohm's law; how series and parallel circuits differ; Kirchhoff's two rules for analysing any network; and how electrical power relates to current and voltage.
bodyHtml:
Electric current is the flow of charge. In metal wires, electrons drift slowly — millimetres per second — but the electric field that pushes them propagates at nearly the speed of light. Current I is measured in amperes (A): 1 A = 1 coulomb of charge per second. By convention, current direction is the flow of positive charge — opposite to electron flow.

Voltage (potential difference) is the energy per unit charge available to do work. A 9 V battery gives each coulomb of charge 9 joules of energy. Resistance R, measured in ohms (Ω), is the opposition to current flow. Ohm's law — V = IR — says the current through a resistor is proportional to the voltage across it. This is a property of ohmic materials (metals at constant temperature); semiconductors and diodes don't follow it.

Components connect in two fundamental ways. In series, the same current flows through everything. Resistances add: R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + R₃. Voltages divide in proportion to resistance. In parallel, the same voltage appears across each branch. Conductances add: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃. Currents divide inversely with resistance — more current flows through the easier path.

Kirchhoff's two rules let you analyse any circuit. The junction rule: total current entering a junction equals total current leaving — charge doesn't accumulate. The loop rule: the algebraic sum of voltage changes around any closed loop is zero — energy is conserved per unit charge. Together they give a set of simultaneous equations you can solve for every current and voltage in the circuit.

Electrical power P = IV = I²R = V²/R, measured in watts. A 60 W bulb on a 240 V supply draws 0.25 A. The I²R form explains why power lines use high voltage: for the same power, higher voltage means lower current, and resistive losses (I²R) drop dramatically. Transformers make this voltage conversion possible with AC.

faqs.q: What's the difference between series and parallel circuits?
faqs.a: In series, components share the same current and their resistances add directly. In parallel, components share the same voltage and their reciprocals add. Series circuits are voltage dividers; parallel circuits are current dividers.

faqs.q: Why does current create heat?
faqs.a: Electrons flowing through a conductor collide with atoms, transferring kinetic energy to the lattice as vibration — which we measure as temperature. The power dissipated is P = I²R. This is useful in a heater but wasteful in transmission lines.

faqs.q: What are Kirchhoff's rules?
faqs.a: The junction rule: current in = current out at any node (charge conservation). The loop rule: sum of voltage rises and drops around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation). Together they provide the equations needed to solve for every unknown current in a circuit.

metaDescription: Master rotational dynamics: torque, moment of inertia, angular momentum, rolling motion, and the rotational analogues of Newton's laws. Free course.
summary: Rotation has its own version of every linear concept. Torque is the rotational analogue of force. Moment of inertia replaces mass. Angular momentum replaces linear momentum. This page builds the parallel between linear and rotational dynamics, so you can solve spinning, rolling, and tumbling problems with the same logic as straight-line motion.
bodyHtml:
When a force makes something spin rather than translate, you're in the domain of torque: τ = r × F, or in magnitude τ = rF sinθ, where r is the vector from the axis to the point of application. A force applied at a larger distance or at a right angle to the lever arm produces more torque. This is why a longer wrench loosens a tight bolt more easily.

Just as net force causes linear acceleration (F = ma), net torque causes angular acceleration: τ_net = Iα, where I is the moment of inertia and α is angular acceleration. Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass — it quantifies how mass is distributed about the axis. A solid disk (I = ½MR²) accelerates faster than a ring of the same mass and radius (I = MR²) under the same torque, because the ring's mass sits farther from the axis.

Parallel-axis theorem: if you know I_cm about the centre of mass, the moment of inertia about any parallel axis distance d away is I = I_cm + Md². This is why a door is easier to push at the handle than near the hinges — the hinge axis is far from the centre of mass.

Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved when no external torque acts — the rotational analogue of linear momentum conservation. This explains the ice skater: pulling arms in reduces I, so ω must increase to keep L constant. The same principle governs spinning neutron stars (pulsars) and the formation of accretion disks around black holes.

For rolling without slipping, the linear and rotational motions are coupled: v = ωR. The total kinetic energy is ½Mv² + ½Iω² = ½Mv²(1 + I/(MR²)). Objects roll down an incline with an effective acceleration reduced by the rotational inertia — a solid sphere beats a hollow sphere, which beats a sliding block (if friction could be turned off). The static friction that prevents slipping does zero work, so mechanical energy is conserved.

faqs.q: What is the difference between torque and force?
faqs.a: Force causes linear acceleration; torque causes angular acceleration. Torque depends not just on how hard you push, but where and at what angle. A given force produces more torque when applied farther from the axis and perpendicular to the lever arm.

faqs.q: Why does an ice skater spin faster when pulling arms in?
faqs.a: Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved (no external torque). Pulling arms in reduces moment of inertia I, so angular velocity ω must increase proportionally. The skater's rotational kinetic energy actually increases — the work comes from the skater's muscles pulling mass inward against centrifugal force.

faqs.q: Which rolls down an incline faster, a solid sphere or a hollow sphere?
faqs.a: The solid sphere. It has a smaller moment of inertia relative to its mass (I = ⅖MR² vs I = ⅔MR² for a hollow sphere), so less of the gravitational potential energy goes into rotation and more into translation. The solid sphere reaches the bottom first.

metaDescription: Understand how light bends and bounces: laws of reflection, Snell's law, total internal reflection, lenses, and optical fibres. Free interactive physics course.
summary: Light changes direction at boundaries between media. Reflection sends it back; refraction bends it forward. These two processes explain mirrors, lenses, rainbows, mirages, and the fibre optics that carry the internet. This page covers the laws that govern both, with the physics of why light slows down in matter.
bodyHtml:
Reflection follows a simple law: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (perpendicular) to the surface. This holds for specular (mirror-like) reflection on smooth surfaces. On rough surfaces, diffuse reflection scatters light in all directions — which is why you can see this page from any angle. Both types obey the same law at the microscopic level.

Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another where its speed differs. Snell's law quantifies this: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, where n is the refractive index — the ratio of light's speed in vacuum (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s) to its speed in the medium. Water has n ≈ 1.33; glass ranges from 1.5 to 1.9. Light slows down in matter because the oscillating electric field makes the atoms' electrons oscillate, and the re-radiated waves interfere with the original to produce a net wave that travels slower.

When light enters a denser medium (higher n), it bends toward the normal. Going from glass to air, it bends away from the normal. At a critical angle θ_c = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁), the refracted angle reaches 90°. Beyond this, total internal reflection occurs — all light reflects back into the denser medium. This is how optical fibres guide light for kilometres with minimal loss, and why diamonds sparkle (high n ≈ 2.42 gives a small critical angle, so light bounces many times inside before escaping).

Dispersion: refractive index varies slightly with wavelength. In most materials, blue light slows more than red, so blue bends more. This is why a prism spreads white light into a spectrum, and why rainbows form — sunlight refracts into water droplets, reflects off the back, and refracts out, with each colour exiting at a slightly different angle.

Lenses use refraction to converge or diverge light. A convex (converging) lens brings parallel rays to a focus at the focal length f. The thin lens equation 1/f = 1/u + 1/v relates object distance u to image distance v. For a magnifying glass, you place the object inside the focal length to get a virtual, enlarged image.

faqs.q: Why does light slow down in glass or water?
faqs.a: The oscillating electric field of the light wave makes electrons in the atoms oscillate. These oscillating charges re-radiate electromagnetic waves that interfere with the original, producing a net wave that propagates more slowly. The frequency stays the same; the wavelength shortens.

faqs.q: What is total internal reflection?
faqs.a: When light travels from a denser to a rarer medium (e.g. glass to air) at an angle greater than the critical angle, all light reflects back — none is transmitted. This is the principle behind optical fibres, endoscopes, and the sparkle of diamonds.

faqs.q: Why does a prism create a rainbow?
faqs.a: The refractive index of glass varies with wavelength — it's slightly higher for blue light than red. So blue bends more at each surface. A prism's geometry amplifies this separation, spreading white light into its constituent colours.

h1: Thermodynamics — heat, work, and the arrow of time
summary: Thermodynamics governs how heat flows, how engines convert thermal energy to work, and why some things can't be undone. This page covers the four laws (zeroth through third), internal energy, the Carnot efficiency limit, entropy as the measure of disorder, and why a cup of tea never spontaneously gets hotter.
bodyHtml:
Thermodynamics studies the relationship between heat, work, and energy at the macroscopic scale. Its power is that it makes no assumptions about microscopic details — it applies equally to steam engines, stars, and living cells.

The zeroth law: if A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other. This defines temperature and justifies thermometers. The first law: ΔU = Q − W. The change in internal energy equals heat added to the system minus work done by the system. It's conservation of energy — you can't get more work out than the energy you put in.

The second law introduces direction. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse (without external work). Entropy S — a measure of the number of microscopic arrangements — never decreases in an isolated system: ΔS ≥ 0. This is why a scrambled egg can't be unscrambled, why perfume diffuses across a room, and why engines can never be 100% efficient.

Carnot's theorem: the maximum possible efficiency of a heat engine operating between a hot reservoir at T_H and a cold reservoir at T_C is η = 1 − T_C/T_H (temperatures in kelvin). No real engine can exceed this. A steam turbine at 800 K exhausting to 300 K has a Carnot limit of 62.5%; real engines achieve less due to friction, turbulence, and heat loss.

The third law: the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero. You can get arbitrarily close to 0 K, but you cannot reach it in a finite number of steps. At extremely low temperatures, quantum effects dominate — helium becomes a superfluid, certain metals superconduct.

Practical thermodynamic processes include isothermal (constant T, ΔU = 0 for ideal gas, Q = W), adiabatic (no heat exchange, Q = 0, ΔU = −W), isochoric (constant volume, W = 0), and isobaric (constant pressure). The Carnot cycle alternates two isothermal and two adiabatic processes to achieve maximum theoretical efficiency.

faqs.q: What is entropy in simple terms?
faqs.a: Entropy measures the number of ways a system's energy can be distributed among its microscopic parts. Higher entropy means more disorder, or more specifically, more possible microscopic arrangements that look the same macroscopically. It always increases in isolated systems — this is why time has a direction.

faqs.q: Why can't an engine be 100% efficient?
faqs.a: The second law requires some heat to be rejected to a cold reservoir — you can't convert all input heat to work. The maximum theoretical efficiency is the Carnot efficiency, 1 − T_C/T_H. To reach 100%, you'd need T_C = 0 K, which the third law forbids.

faqs.q: What's the difference between heat and temperature?
faqs.a: Temperature (kelvin) measures the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance. Heat (joules) is the total thermal energy transferred between systems due to a temperature difference. A spark has high temperature but little heat; a warm ocean has modest temperature but enormous heat content.

subject: physics
metaDescription: How gravity holds planets in orbit: Newton's law, g vs G, Kepler's laws, escape velocity and weightlessness — explained simply, with a free interactive course.
summary: Gravity is the architect of the cosmos. From an apple falling to the ground to a galaxy spinning 100,000 light-years across, the same inverse-square law governs it all. This page covers Newton's universal law of gravitation, Kepler's three laws of planetary motion, escape velocity, gravitational potential energy, and why satellites stay up.
bodyHtml:
Newton's universal law of gravitation: every point mass attracts every other with F = Gm₁m₂/r². The constant G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg² is extraordinarily small — the gravitational attraction between two 1 kg masses 1 m apart is just 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N, about the weight of a single bacterium. But because Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, the cumulative pull is 9.8 N on every kilogram at the surface.

Kepler's three laws, discovered empirically from Tycho Brahe's data, were explained by Newton's gravitational theory. First law: planets orbit in ellipses with the Sun at one focus (not circles — though most planetary orbits are nearly circular). Second law (equal areas in equal times): a planet moves faster when closer to the Sun, sweeping out equal areas in equal time intervals. Third law: T² ∝ a³, where T is orbital period and a is semi-major axis. For circular orbits, setting gravitational force equal to centripetal force gives T² = (4π²/GM)a³.

Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to leave a body's gravitational field without further propulsion: v_esc = √(2GM/R). For Earth, it's about 11.2 km/s. For a black hole, the escape velocity at the event horizon equals the speed of light — nothing can escape. Note that escape velocity doesn't depend on the escaping object's mass.

Gravitational potential energy for large distances is U = −Gm₁m₂/r. The negative sign means the system is bound — you must add energy to separate the masses to infinity. This formula replaces mgh, which only works near Earth's surface. The total mechanical energy of a satellite in a circular orbit is E = −GMm/(2r) — exactly half the potential energy and the negative of the kinetic energy.

Weightlessness in orbit is not the absence of gravity. At 400 km altitude (ISS), g is still about 8.7 m/s² — 89% of surface value. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are in continuous free fall around Earth, with no contact force pushing on their feet. They feel weightless for the same reason you feel weightless at the top of a roller coaster drop.

faqs.q: What is the difference between g and G?
faqs.a: g is the local gravitational field strength (~9.8 N/kg at Earth's surface); G is the universal gravitational constant (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹), the same everywhere. They are related by g = GM/R² at a given planet's surface.

faqs.q: Why do astronauts feel weightless in orbit?
faqs.a: They are in continuous free fall around Earth together with their spacecraft, so there is no contact force to feel — not because gravity is absent. Gravity at ISS altitude is still about 89% of its surface value.

faqs.q: How did Kepler know orbits are elliptical?
faqs.a: Kepler analysed decades of precise planetary position measurements made by Tycho Brahe. Mars's orbit showed the clearest deviation from a circle. Trying to fit a circular orbit left an 8-arcminute discrepancy — Kepler trusted the data and discovered the ellipse, which fit perfectly.

metaDescription: Learn the three modes of heat transfer: conduction (solids), convection (fluids), and radiation (electromagnetic). Free interactive physics course.
h1: Heat transfer — conduction, convection, and radiation
summary: Heat moves in three ways. Conduction carries it through solids by atomic vibrations and free electrons. Convection carries it through fluids by bulk motion. Radiation carries it through empty space as electromagnetic waves. This page explains all three with the equations that govern them and how they show up in everyday life.
bodyHtml:
Conduction is heat transfer through a material without bulk motion of the material itself. In metals, free electrons carry kinetic energy from hot regions to cold regions efficiently — this is why a metal spoon in hot tea gets hot at the handle. Fourier's law quantifies it: the heat flow rate H = kA ΔT/L, where k is thermal conductivity, A is cross-sectional area, ΔT is the temperature difference, and L is the thickness. Copper (k ≈ 400 W/m·K) conducts heat about 20,000 times faster than still air (k ≈ 0.026 W/m·K) — which is why double-glazed windows trap an insulating air gap.

Convection is heat transfer by the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas). When a fluid is heated from below, it expands, becomes less dense, and rises. Cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace it, setting up a convection current. This is how a pot of water boils, how a radiator heats a room, and how Earth's mantle drives plate tectonics. The rate depends on the temperature difference, fluid properties, and geometry — captured in the dimensionless Nusselt and Rayleigh numbers.

Convection can be natural (driven by density differences from heating) or forced (driven by a pump or fan). Your laptop's fan is forced convection; the rising plume above a candle is natural convection. Forced convection transfers heat much faster, which is why blowing on hot soup cools it more quickly.

Radiation is heat transfer by electromagnetic waves — no medium needed. Every object above absolute zero emits thermal radiation. The Stefan–Boltzmann law gives the power radiated: P = εσAT⁴, where ε is emissivity (0–1), σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴, and T is in kelvin. Because of the T⁴ dependence, doubling the absolute temperature increases radiated power by 16 times. The Sun's surface at ~5800 K radiates about 64 MW per square metre. The colour of the radiation shifts with temperature — red-hot iron, yellow Sun, blue-hot stars — described by Wien's displacement law: λ_max = b/T.

In the real world, all three modes often act together. A thermos flask fights all three: a vacuum between double walls stops conduction and convection; silvered surfaces reflect radiation. The Earth's climate also involves all three, with greenhouse gases trapping outgoing infrared radiation while incoming visible light passes through.

faqs.q: Why do metals feel colder than wood at the same temperature?
faqs.a: Metals have high thermal conductivity — they rapidly conduct heat away from your skin, cooling the skin surface quickly. Wood has low conductivity, so it draws heat slowly. Both are at the same temperature; your sensation is of heat flow rate, not temperature.

faqs.q: Why is space cold if the Sun is so hot?
faqs.a: Space is largely empty — there's nothing to have a temperature. Objects in space reach an equilibrium temperature where absorbed solar radiation equals emitted thermal radiation. Near Earth, this is about 280 K (7 °C). In shadow or deep space, an object radiates without receiving much, cooling toward ~3 K (the cosmic microwave background).

faqs.q: How does a thermos flask keep things hot or cold?
faqs.a: It attacks all three heat transfer modes: a vacuum between two glass walls eliminates conduction and convection; silvered surfaces reflect thermal radiation; a tight stopper prevents convection through the opening. The only remaining heat path is through the thin glass at the neck and through the stopper.

metaDescription: Understand magnetic fields, forces on moving charges, Faraday's law, Lenz's law, inductance, and how generators and transformers work. Free course.
summary: Magnetism and electricity are two sides of the same phenomenon. Moving charges create magnetic fields; changing magnetic fields create electric currents. This page covers the force on a current-carrying wire, the Biot–Savart law, Faraday's law of induction, Lenz's law, and how these principles power every generator and transformer on the grid.
bodyHtml:
Magnetic fields exert forces on moving charges. The Lorentz force on a charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B is F = qv × B. Because it's a cross product, the force is perpendicular to both v and B — magnetic forces change direction but not speed. This is why charged particles spiral around magnetic field lines, and why a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a sideways force F = IL × B.

Magnetic fields themselves are produced by moving charges. A straight wire carrying current I produces circular field lines around it with magnitude B = μ₀I/(2πr) at distance r. A solenoid (coil) produces a nearly uniform field inside: B = μ₀nI, where n is turns per unit length. The constant μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ N/A² is the permeability of free space.

Faraday's law of induction: a changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an emf (voltage) equal to the negative rate of change of flux: ε = −dΦ_B/dt. This is the principle behind every generator — spin a coil in a magnetic field, and the changing flux drives current. It's also why moving a magnet through a coil lights a bulb.

Lenz's law gives the minus sign in Faraday's law: the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. If you push a magnet toward a coil, the induced current creates a magnetic field that repels the magnet. This is not a violation of energy conservation — the opposition is what requires you to do work to push the magnet, and that work becomes electrical energy.

Inductance L quantifies a coil's opposition to changes in current: ε = −L dI/dt. An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field: U = ½LI². In an LR circuit, the current doesn't jump instantly — it rises or decays exponentially with time constant τ = L/R. Transformers use mutual inductance: an alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing flux that induces voltage in the secondary. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. This is how the grid steps voltage up for transmission and down for home use.

faqs.q: Why does a changing magnetic field produce current?
faqs.a: A changing magnetic flux creates a circulating electric field (Faraday's law). This electric field pushes charges around a conducting loop, producing current. It's a fundamental relationship — one of Maxwell's equations — not derivable from anything simpler.

faqs.q: How does a generator work?
faqs.a: Mechanical energy spins a coil of wire in a magnetic field. The changing orientation means the magnetic flux through the coil changes continuously, inducing an alternating emf. The mechanical work done to overcome magnetic forces becomes electrical energy.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a motor and a generator?
faqs.a: A motor converts electrical energy to mechanical rotation: current in a magnetic field experiences torque. A generator does the reverse: mechanical rotation changes flux and induces current. Physically, they're the same device run in opposite directions — many electric vehicles use the same unit for both driving and regenerative braking.

metaDescription: Apply differentiation to physics: instantaneous velocity and acceleration, related rates, maxima and minima in mechanics, and differential equations of motion. Free course.
summary: Differentiation turns position into velocity and velocity into acceleration. It finds maxima and minima — the peak height of a projectile, the minimum force for equilibrium. It relates rates of change when quantities are linked. This page shows how calculus translates physical intuition into precise, solvable mathematical form.
bodyHtml:
Kinematics with derivatives: if position is given as a function of time, r(t), then velocity v(t) = dr/dt and acceleration a(t) = dv/dt = d²r/dt². A particle whose position is r(t) = (3t²)î + (2t³)ĵ has velocity v(t) = (6t)î + (6t²)ĵ and acceleration a(t) = 6î + (12t)ĵ. The derivative gives the instantaneous rate — the speedometer reading at a single moment, not the average over a trip.

Optimisation problems use derivatives to find extreme values. To maximise the range of a projectile on an incline, differentiate the range expression with respect to launch angle and set the derivative to zero. To find the minimum work to raise a bucket from a well while its rope weighs it down, set up W(h) and differentiate. The derivative vanishes at a maximum or minimum — the sign of the second derivative tells you which.

Related rates: when two quantities are linked by an equation, their rates of change are linked by implicit differentiation. A ladder sliding down a wall: x² + y² = L². Differentiate with respect to time: 2x(dx/dt) + 2y(dy/dt) = 0, so dy/dt = −(x/y)(dx/dt). If the base slides out at 2 m/s when the top is 3 m high, you can compute how fast the top descends without solving for y(t) explicitly.

Newton's second law written as a differential equation: m(d²x/dt²) = ΣF(x, v, t). For a spring, F = −kx, giving d²x/dt² = −(k/m)x — the simple harmonic oscillator equation. Its solutions are sines and cosines. For damping, add a term −b(dx/dt), giving d²x/dt² + (b/m)(dx/dt) + (k/m)x = 0, which produces exponential decay of oscillations. These equations model everything from car suspensions to building sway in earthquakes.

The chain rule is essential in physics. Acceleration can be written as a = v(dv/dx) — useful when force depends on position rather than time. For a body falling with air resistance proportional to v, you can solve dv/dt = g − kv by separation of variables to get v(t) = (g/k)(1 − e^{−kt}), showing the approach to terminal velocity.

faqs.q: Why do we use derivatives in physics?
faqs.a: Physics deals with rates of change — velocity is the rate of change of position, acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Derivatives give us the instantaneous rate at a single moment, which is what physical laws describe. Newton invented calculus precisely to solve physics problems.

faqs.q: How do I solve related rates problems?
faqs.a: Write the equation linking the quantities, differentiate both sides with respect to time (using the chain rule), substitute the known values and rates, and solve for the unknown rate. The key step is implicit differentiation — you treat each variable as a function of time.

faqs.q: What is terminal velocity and how does calculus describe it?
faqs.a: Terminal velocity is the constant speed a falling object reaches when air resistance equals weight. From the differential equation m(dv/dt) = mg − kv, set dv/dt = 0 to find v_terminal = mg/k. The full solution v(t) = v_terminal(1 − e^{−kt/m}) shows the exponential approach.

subject: physics
metaDescription: Apply integration to physics: work as ∫F·dx, centre of mass, moment of inertia, impulse, and areas under curves. Free interactive physics course.
summary: Integration accumulates small contributions into a total. In physics, that means work from a varying force, mass from a varying density, the centre of mass of a continuous body, impulse from a time-varying force, and electric fields from continuous charge distributions. This page shows how integration turns local laws into global predictions.
bodyHtml:
Where differentiation breaks things into instants, integration adds them back up. Velocity is the integral of acceleration: v(t) = v₀ + ∫a(t) dt. Position is the integral of velocity: x(t) = x₀ + ∫v(t) dt. If you know acceleration as a function of time, two integrations (and two initial conditions) give the complete trajectory.

Work from a varying force: W = ∫F·dx. When force is constant, this reduces to F Δx. But when you stretch a spring, the force grows linearly: F = kx. The work done in stretching from 0 to x is W = ∫₀ˣ kx dx = ½kx² — which becomes the spring's stored potential energy. Similarly, the work to lift an object against gravity that weakens with height (F = GMm/r²) requires integrating the inverse-square force.

Centre of mass for a continuous body: R = (1/M)∫r dm. For a uniform rod, the centre is at the midpoint. For a triangular plate, it's at the intersection of medians (⅓ of the way up from the base). The integration accounts for how mass is distributed — each bit of mass contributes to the average position in proportion to its size.

Moment of inertia: I = ∫r² dm. Each mass element contributes in proportion to the square of its distance from the axis. A thin rod about its end has I = ⅓ML²; about its centre, I = (1/12)ML². The difference illustrates the parallel-axis theorem: I_end = I_cm + M(L/2)² = (1/12)ML² + ¼ML² = ⅓ML².

In electrostatics, integration sums contributions from continuous charge distributions. The electric field from a line of charge is the integral of dE = (k dq)/r² contributions from each infinitesimal segment. Symmetry often simplifies these — a uniformly charged ring produces zero net field at its centre by cancellation, but the on-axis field requires integrating only the axial components.

Impulse from a time-varying force: J = ∫F(t) dt = Δp. This is the general form — the impulse–momentum theorem. For a force that spikes during a collision and returns to zero, the integral (area under the force–time curve) gives the total momentum change. The average force multiplied by duration gives the same integral — this is why extending collision time reduces average force.

faqs.q: Why do we need integration in physics?
faqs.a: Many physical quantities involve summing infinitesimal contributions: work from a changing force, total mass of an object with varying density, electric field from a continuous charge distribution. Integration is the mathematical tool for performing these sums exactly.

faqs.q: How is the moment of inertia different from mass?
faqs.a: Mass quantifies resistance to linear acceleration. Moment of inertia quantifies resistance to angular acceleration. It depends not just on how much mass there is, but on how far each bit of mass is from the rotation axis — hence the r² in I = ∫r² dm.

faqs.q: What's the relationship between integration and differentiation in physics?
faqs.a: They're inverse operations. Velocity is the derivative of position and position is the integral of velocity. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, and velocity is the integral of acceleration. Which you use depends on what you're given and what you need: derivatives when you have position and need velocity; integrals when you have acceleration and need trajectory.

metaDescription: Learn applied mechanics: simple machines, hydraulic systems, fluid pressure, buoyancy, stress and strain, and material properties. Free interactive course.
h1: Applied mechanics — machines, fluids, and materials
summary: Mechanics principles meet the real world. This page covers simple machines (levers, pulleys, screws), how fluids transmit pressure (Pascal's principle), why things float (Archimedes), and how materials respond to forces (stress, strain, Young's modulus). These are the physics behind every tool, hydraulic system, and structure.
bodyHtml:
Simple machines trade force for distance. A lever: effort × effort arm = load × load arm. A movable pulley halves the force needed but doubles the rope you must pull. An inclined plane lets you raise a load with less force over a longer path: F = mg sinθ. A hydraulic press uses Pascal's principle — pressure is transmitted undiminished through a fluid — so a small force on a small piston balances a large force on a large piston: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂. The work input equals work output (ignoring friction) — you never get something for nothing.

Fluid statics: pressure in a fluid increases with depth: P = P₀ + ρgh, where ρ is density and h is depth. At 10 m underwater, pressure is roughly 2 atmospheres — the atmosphere above plus the water column. Buoyancy (Archimedes' principle): a body submerged in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of fluid displaced. A ship floats because its hull displaces water weighing more than the ship itself. A hot-air balloon rises because the heated air inside is less dense than the surrounding cool air.

Fluid dynamics: for an ideal (inviscid, incompressible) fluid in steady flow, the continuity equation A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ says flow rate is constant — fluid speeds up through narrow sections. Bernoulli's equation P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline. This explains why a fast-moving fluid exerts lower pressure — the principle behind aeroplane wings, atomisers, and why a shower curtain gets sucked inward when the water runs.

Material mechanics: stress σ = F/A (force per unit area, measured in pascals). Strain ε = ΔL/L (fractional deformation, dimensionless). For many materials in the elastic regime, stress is proportional to strain: σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus. Steel has E ≈ 200 GPa; rubber has E ≈ 0.01 GPa. Beyond the elastic limit, deformation becomes permanent (plastic). The ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress before fracture.

Real materials also show shear (sliding deformation, governed by shear modulus G) and bulk compression (volume change under uniform pressure, governed by bulk modulus B). Poisson's ratio ν describes how a material thins when stretched — cork has ν ≈ 0 (ideal for bottle stoppers), rubber ν ≈ 0.5 (nearly incompressible).

faqs.q: How does a hydraulic press multiply force?
faqs.a: Pascal's principle: pressure in an enclosed fluid is the same everywhere. A small force on a small-area piston creates pressure P = F₁/A₁. That same pressure acts on a large-area piston to produce force F₂ = P × A₂ = F₁(A₂/A₁). The area ratio multiplies the force — but the small piston must move farther (work is conserved).

faqs.q: Why does a steel ship float?
faqs.a: Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of displaced water. A solid steel block sinks because it displaces less water than its weight. But a hollow steel ship displaces a volume of water whose weight equals the ship's total weight — the ship's average density (including the air inside) is less than water's.

faqs.q: What's the difference between stress and strain?
faqs.a: Stress is force per unit area (measured in pascals) — it's the cause. Strain is the resulting fractional deformation (dimensionless) — it's the effect. In the elastic regime, they're proportional: stress = Young's modulus × strain. Two different materials under the same stress will have different strains depending on their stiffness.
