metaDescription: Understand simple harmonic motion, damped and forced oscillations, resonance, wave propagation, sound waves, and the physics of music. Free interactive course.
summary: Oscillations are everywhere: a pendulum swinging, a guitar string vibrating, an electrical circuit ringing, a bridge wobbling in the wind. Acoustics is the physics of sound — oscillations that propagate through a medium. This page covers the mathematics of simple harmonic motion, damping, resonance, and how vibrating objects create the sounds we hear.
bodyHtml:
Simple harmonic motion (SHM) occurs when the restoring force is proportional to displacement and opposite in direction: F = −kx. The equation of motion is d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0, where ω = √(k/m) is the angular frequency. Solutions are sinusoidal: x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ). The period T = 2π/ω is independent of amplitude — an ideal pendulum's period depends only on its length and g, not on how wide it swings (for small angles).

In SHM, energy continuously swaps between kinetic and potential. At maximum displacement, all energy is potential (½kA²). At equilibrium, all energy is kinetic (½mv²_max). The total energy ½kA² is constant. The velocity at any point is v = ω√(A² − x²).

Damping removes energy from an oscillator. With a velocity-dependent drag force −bv, the amplitude decays exponentially: A(t) = A₀ e^{−γt}, where γ = b/(2m). Three regimes exist: underdamped (oscillates while decaying), critically damped (returns to equilibrium fastest without oscillating), and overdamped (returns slowly without oscillating). Car suspensions are designed near critical damping.

Forced oscillations and resonance: when you push an oscillator at its natural frequency ω₀, the amplitude grows dramatically — this is resonance. The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse (1940) is the classic cautionary tale. Soldiers break step when crossing bridges for the same reason. The quality factor Q = ω₀/Δω measures how sharply an oscillator resonates: high Q means a narrow, tall resonance peak.

Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave in a medium. In air at 20 °C, sound travels at about 343 m/s. The speed depends on the medium's stiffness and density: faster in solids, slower in gases. A sound wave is described by its frequency f (pitch), wavelength λ (v = fλ), and amplitude (loudness — measured in decibels on a logarithmic scale). Standing waves on a string or in a pipe produce the notes of musical instruments: the fundamental frequency and its integer-multiple harmonics. The pattern of harmonics (timbre) is what distinguishes a violin from a flute playing the same note.

faqs.q: What is resonance and why is it dangerous?
faqs.a: Resonance occurs when a system is driven at its natural frequency, causing large-amplitude oscillations. It's dangerous in structures because the energy accumulates cycle after cycle until the material fails — like pushing a swing at just the right moment to go higher each time.

faqs.q: Why does sound travel faster in solids than in air?
faqs.a: Sound speed depends on the stiffness and density of the medium. Solids have much stronger interatomic bonds (higher effective stiffness), so disturbances propagate faster. In steel, sound travels at about 5000 m/s — roughly 15 times faster than in air.

faqs.q: What determines the pitch of a musical note?
faqs.a: Pitch is determined by frequency: higher frequency = higher pitch. For a stringed instrument, frequency depends on length (shorter = higher), tension (tighter = higher), and mass per unit length (lighter string = higher). For a wind instrument, frequency depends on the length of the air column.

metaDescription: Learn applied electricity: how batteries work, AC vs DC, RMS values, transformers, power transmission, and the physics of radio communication. Free course.
h1: Applied electricity — batteries, AC, and radio
summary: Electricity powers modern life, and AC makes long-distance transmission possible. This page covers how chemical cells produce steady voltage, why the grid runs on alternating current, what RMS means, how transformers step voltage up and down, and how radio waves carry information by modulating a carrier signal.
bodyHtml:
DC sources drive current in one direction. A battery converts chemical energy to electrical: in a simple cell, two different metals in an electrolyte create a potential difference through redox reactions. The emf (electromotive force, measured in volts) is the energy per unit charge the cell provides. Real batteries have internal resistance r, so the terminal voltage is V = ε − Ir — it drops when more current is drawn.

Alternating current (AC) oscillates direction, typically sinusoidally: V(t) = V₀ sin(ωt), I(t) = I₀ sin(ωt − φ). The phase difference φ arises from reactive components — inductors make current lag voltage; capacitors make current lead. Since the average of sin²(ωt) over a cycle is ½, the RMS (root mean square) values are V_rms = V₀/√2 and I_rms = I₀/√2. A 230 V mains supply peaks at about 325 V. RMS is the DC voltage that would deliver the same average power to a resistor: P_avg = V_rms I_rms = I²_rms R.

AC dominates power grids because transformers can change its voltage efficiently. A transformer uses two coils on a shared iron core: an alternating current in the primary creates changing magnetic flux that induces voltage in the secondary. Voltage ratio equals turns ratio: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. Power is (ideally) conserved, so current transforms inversely: I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s. This lets the grid step up to hundreds of kilovolts for low-loss transmission (minimising I²R heating), then step down for safe home use.

In AC circuits, resistors, inductors, and capacitors each respond to frequency differently. Reactance: X_L = ωL (grows with frequency), X_C = 1/(ωC) (shrinks with frequency). Impedance Z combines resistance and reactance: for an RLC series circuit, Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²). Resonance occurs when X_L = X_C, giving minimum impedance and maximum current.

Radio encodes information onto a high-frequency carrier wave. In AM (amplitude modulation), the carrier's amplitude varies with the audio signal. In FM (frequency modulation), the carrier's frequency shifts slightly. The modulated wave is transmitted, and the receiver extracts (demodulates) the original signal. The antenna length is matched to the wavelength — a half-wave dipole for 100 MHz FM radio is about 1.5 m long.

faqs.q: Why does the power grid use AC instead of DC?
faqs.a: AC voltage can be changed easily with transformers — step up for efficient long-distance transmission, step down for safe use. DC voltage conversion is more complex and was historically less efficient. High-voltage DC transmission is now gaining ground for very long distances or undersea cables.

faqs.q: What does RMS voltage mean?
faqs.a: RMS (root mean square) is the effective value of an alternating voltage or current — the DC equivalent that would deliver the same average power to a resistor. For a sine wave, V_rms = V_peak/√2 ≈ 0.707 V_peak. UK mains at 230 V RMS peaks at about 325 V.

faqs.q: How does a radio wave carry sound?
faqs.a: A high-frequency carrier wave (e.g. 100 MHz for FM radio) has one of its properties varied in step with the audio signal. In AM, the amplitude varies. In FM, the frequency shifts slightly. The receiver extracts this modulation pattern and amplifies it to drive a speaker.

subject: physics
metaDescription: Explore gyroscopic precession, magnetic materials, interference, diffraction, and polarisation — advanced topics across rotational and wave physics. Free course.
summary: Three advanced topics spanning rotation, electromagnetism, and light. A spinning gyroscope defies intuition by precessing instead of falling. Magnetic materials range from iron to superconductors. Wave optics reveals that light interferes, diffracts, and polarises — proving it's a wave. This page connects the key ideas across these domains.
bodyHtml:
Gyroscopic precession is the puzzling behaviour of a spinning top: instead of falling over, it slowly circles around the vertical. The explanation is torque and angular momentum. Gravity exerts a torque τ = r × mg that is horizontal, perpendicular to the angular momentum L. Since τ = dL/dt, the change in L is perpendicular to L itself — so L rotates (precesses) rather than changing magnitude. The precession angular velocity is Ω = mgr/(Iω): the faster the spin, the slower the precession.

Magnetic materials: not all substances respond to magnets the same way. Diamagnetic materials (water, copper, most organic matter) are weakly repelled — they create an opposing field when exposed to an external magnet. Paramagnetic materials (aluminium, oxygen) are weakly attracted — unpaired electrons align with the field. Ferromagnetic materials (iron, nickel, cobalt) can be permanently magnetised because quantum exchange interactions align neighbouring atomic dipoles even without an external field. Above the Curie temperature, thermal agitation destroys this alignment and ferromagnets become paramagnetic.

Interference: when two coherent light waves overlap, their amplitudes add. Constructive interference (bright fringe) occurs when the path difference is an integer number of wavelengths: Δr = mλ. Destructive interference (dark fringe) at Δr = (m + ½)λ. Young's double-slit experiment (1801) was the definitive proof that light is a wave. The fringe spacing is Δy = λD/d, where D is the slit-to-screen distance and d is the slit separation.

Diffraction: waves bend around obstacles and spread through apertures. A single slit of width a produces a central bright band of angular width 2λ/a flanked by dimmer fringes. A diffraction grating — many equally spaced slits — produces sharp spectral lines at angles satisfying d sinθ = mλ, separating light into its component wavelengths for spectroscopy.

Polarisation: light is a transverse electromagnetic wave. Unpolarised light vibrates in all transverse directions equally. A polarising filter transmits only one direction of vibration. Two crossed polarisers block all light. Reflection from a non-metallic surface at Brewster's angle produces fully polarised reflected light — the basis of polarising sunglasses, which cut glare from horizontal surfaces.

faqs.q: Why doesn't a spinning gyroscope fall over?
faqs.a: Gravity produces a torque perpendicular to the spin axis. Torque equals rate of change of angular momentum (τ = dL/dt), so the change is perpendicular to L itself. Instead of tipping, the gyroscope precesses — its axis rotates around the vertical. The faster it spins, the slower it precesses.

faqs.q: What's the difference between interference and diffraction?
faqs.a: Interference is the superposition of waves from a small number of discrete sources (like two slits). Diffraction is the bending and spreading of waves when they encounter an obstacle or aperture — it can be understood as interference from infinitely many sources across the wavefront. They're the same fundamental phenomenon at different scales.

faqs.q: How do polarised sunglasses reduce glare?
faqs.a: Light reflecting off a horizontal surface (water, road) becomes partially horizontally polarised. Polarised sunglasses have vertically oriented filters that block this horizontal component, cutting glare while transmitting most other light.

seoTitle: Newtonian Mechanics — The Full Picture — Qubix
metaDescription: A thorough treatment of Newtonian mechanics: kinematics, dynamics, conservation laws, gravitation, and solving mechanics problems systematically. Free course.
summary: Newtonian mechanics is the complete framework for understanding motion at everyday scales. This page integrates kinematics, Newton's laws, conservation principles (energy, momentum, angular momentum), and gravitational theory into a unified problem-solving approach. If you want to think like a physicist when a mechanics problem appears, this is the toolkit.
bodyHtml:
Newtonian mechanics rests on three pillars: kinematics (describing motion), dynamics (Newton's laws linking forces to motion), and conservation laws (energy, momentum, angular momentum — each a shortcut that bypasses the detailed forces).

Kinematics gives the vocabulary. Position r(t), velocity v = dr/dt, acceleration a = dv/dt. For constant acceleration in one dimension: v = v₀ + at, x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², v² = v₀² + 2aΔx. Projectile motion separates into independent horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (constant acceleration g) components — the key insight that makes these problems solvable.

Dynamics adds causes. Newton's first law: objects maintain constant velocity unless acted upon by a net force. Second law: F = dp/dt = ma (for constant mass). Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies. The free-body diagram — isolating one object and drawing every force as an arrow — is the universal starting point. With the forces identified, write F_net = ma in component form for each direction and solve.

The conservation laws are consequences of Newton's laws with specific conditions. Momentum is conserved when the net external force is zero — invaluable for collisions. Angular momentum L = r × p is conserved when net external torque is zero — explaining everything from spinning skaters to planetary orbits. Mechanical energy (KE + PE) is conserved when only conservative forces do work — letting you trade height for speed with simple algebra rather than solving differential equations.

The framework unifies apparently disparate phenomena. A planet orbiting the Sun and a ball on a string both obey F = ma with a central force. A block sliding down an incline and a pendulum swinging both trade gravitational potential for kinetic energy. The same vector cross product gives torque (r × F) and angular momentum (r × p). Learn the patterns rather than memorising each case separately, and mechanics becomes a single coherent subject.

faqs.q: What are the limits of Newtonian mechanics?
faqs.a: Newtonian mechanics fails for speeds near the speed of light (use special relativity), for very strong gravitational fields (use general relativity), and at atomic scales (use quantum mechanics). For everyday speeds, sizes, and gravity — from engineering to orbital mechanics — it's extraordinarily accurate.

faqs.q: Why are conservation laws so useful?
faqs.a: They let you relate initial and final states directly without solving for the detailed motion in between. If only conservative forces act, the speed of a roller coaster at the bottom of a drop depends only on the height lost, not the shape of the track.

faqs.q: How do I approach any mechanics problem systematically?
faqs.a: Draw a clear diagram. Isolate the object(s) of interest with free-body diagrams. Choose a convenient coordinate system. Write F = ma in component form for each object. Count equations and unknowns. Bring in constraints (inextensible strings, rolling without slipping) and conservation laws if they simplify things. Solve.

subject: physics
metaDescription: Rotational dynamics meets thermodynamics: torque, moment of inertia, angular momentum, kinetic theory, laws of thermodynamics, and heat engines. Free course.
summary: This page connects two major domains of classical physics. Rotational dynamics extends Newton's laws to spinning, rolling, and tumbling objects. Thermodynamics governs heat, work, and entropy at the macroscopic scale. Together they cover everything from a spinning flywheel storing energy to a steam engine converting heat to work.
bodyHtml:
Rotational kinematics mirrors linear kinematics: angular displacement θ replaces x, angular velocity ω replaces v, angular acceleration α replaces a. The equations are identical in form: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = ω₀t + ½αt², ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ.

Rotational dynamics introduces torque (τ = r × F), moment of inertia (I = ∫r² dm), and angular momentum (L = Iω). Newton's second law for rotation: τ_net = Iα. Angular momentum is conserved when net external torque is zero. A gyroscope precesses because gravity's torque changes the direction of L, not its magnitude — the same principle that keeps a bicycle upright when the wheels are spinning.

For rolling without slipping, v = ωR and a = αR. The total kinetic energy splits between translation (½Mv²) and rotation (½Iω²). Objects with larger I/MR² accelerate slower down an incline because more gravitational potential diverts into rotation.

Kinetic theory connects the microscopic world of molecules to macroscopic thermodynamics. The pressure of an ideal gas arises from countless molecular collisions with the walls: P = (1/3)ρ⟨v²⟩. The average translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)k_B T, where k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K. Temperature is a measure of average molecular kinetic energy.

Thermodynamics adds the macroscopic laws. First law: ΔU = Q − W (energy conservation at the system level). Second law: heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold; entropy of an isolated system never decreases; no heat engine can be 100% efficient. The Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T_C/T_H sets the theoretical maximum for any engine operating between two temperatures. Real engines (Otto, Diesel, Rankine cycles) approach this limit through different pressure–volume paths.

The two domains connect through thermodynamic processes: isothermal (constant T), adiabatic (no heat exchange, PV^γ = constant for ideal gas), isochoric (constant V), and isobaric (constant P). The work done in a PV diagram is the area under the curve — a geometric interpretation that makes cycle analysis visual.

faqs.q: What's the relationship between rotation and thermodynamics?
faqs.a: They're connected through statistical mechanics — the kinetic theory of gases links molecular rotation and translation to temperature and pressure. Practically, rotating machinery (turbines, flywheels) converts between rotational kinetic energy and thermal energy in thermodynamic cycles.

faqs.q: What is moment of inertia and why does it matter?
faqs.a: Moment of inertia I is the rotational analogue of mass — it quantifies resistance to angular acceleration. It depends on both the total mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the rotation axis. The same mass farther from the axis gives larger I and slower acceleration under the same torque.

faqs.q: How does a heat engine convert heat to work?
faqs.a: A working substance (gas) absorbs heat Q_H from a hot reservoir, expands and does work, then rejects waste heat Q_C to a cold reservoir. The net work output is Q_H − Q_C. The second law requires Q_C > 0 — you can't convert all the input heat to work. The maximum efficiency is the Carnot limit.

h1: Optics — light, lenses, and optical instruments
summary: Optics is the study of light and how it interacts with mirrors, lenses, and prisms to form images. This page covers the ray model of light, the mirror and lens equations, magnification, how the eye focuses, and how telescopes and microscopes extend our vision from galaxies to cells.
bodyHtml:
Geometrical optics models light as rays travelling in straight lines, bending only at interfaces (reflection or refraction). This model works when objects and apertures are much larger than the wavelength of light — it describes mirrors, lenses, and everyday imaging perfectly.

Mirrors: a plane mirror produces a virtual, upright, same-size image behind the mirror at equal distance. A concave spherical mirror (like a makeup mirror) can produce a magnified virtual image when the object is inside the focal length. The mirror equation: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, where f = R/2 for a spherical mirror. Magnification m = −v/u (negative means inverted).

Lenses refract light to converge or diverge rays. A convex (converging) lens is thicker at the centre — it brings parallel rays to a real focus. A concave (diverging) lens is thinner at the centre — it spreads parallel rays as if from a virtual focus. The thin lens equation 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, with sign conventions: u is positive for real objects, v is positive for real images (on the opposite side of the lens from the object), f is positive for converging lenses. The lensmaker's formula 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂) connects focal length to refractive index and surface curvatures.

The human eye forms an image on the retina using a variable-focus lens. The near point (closest comfortable focus) is about 25 cm for a young adult. Myopia (short-sightedness) means the eye's lens is too strong or the eyeball too long — distant objects focus in front of the retina, corrected by diverging lenses. Hyperopia (long-sightedness) is the opposite, corrected by converging lenses.

Optical instruments combine lenses. A simple magnifier (single converging lens) gives angular magnification M = 25/f (for f in cm). A compound microscope uses an objective lens (short focal length, high magnification) and an eyepiece (moderate focal length), giving total magnification M = M_obj × M_ep. A refracting telescope uses a long-focal-length objective and a short-focal-length eyepiece: angular magnification M = f_obj/f_ep. The aperture determines light-gathering power and diffraction-limited resolution.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a real and virtual image?
faqs.a: A real image is formed when rays actually converge at a point — you can project it onto a screen. A virtual image is formed when rays only appear to diverge from a point — you can see it but can't project it. A plane mirror produces virtual images; a projector lens produces real images.

faqs.q: How does a telescope magnify distant objects?
faqs.a: The objective lens (or mirror) forms a real image of the distant object at its focal plane. The eyepiece acts as a magnifier to view that image. The angular magnification is the ratio of focal lengths: M = f_objective / f_eyepiece. A larger objective also collects more light, making faint objects visible.

faqs.q: Why is the image in a concave mirror upside down?
faqs.a: When the object is beyond the focal point, rays from the top of the object reflect through the focal point and cross the axis below it. The image is inverted because of this ray crossing. When the object is inside the focal length (like a makeup mirror), rays don't cross and the image is upright and virtual.

metaDescription: Learn about DC motors, generators, transformers, measuring instruments, and the physics behind electrical machines used in engineering. Free course.
summary: This page bridges physics principles and practical engineering. DC motors turn current into rotation; generators do the reverse. Transformers change voltage. Measuring instruments — ammeters, voltmeters, oscilloscopes — quantify what's happening in a circuit. Understanding how these devices work physically, not just how to use them, is the difference between an operator and an engineer.
bodyHtml:
DC motors use the Lorentz force on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field. The force F = IL × B on each side of the coil produces a torque. A split-ring commutator reverses the current direction every half-turn, keeping the torque in the same rotational direction. The back emf — induced as the coil spins in the magnetic field (Faraday's law) — opposes the applied voltage and limits the motor's speed. At no load, the motor speeds up until the back emf nearly equals the supply voltage. Under load, it slows, back emf drops, and current increases to deliver more torque.

Generators are motors run backward: mechanical rotation changes the magnetic flux through coils, inducing an emf. A DC generator uses the same split-ring commutator to produce pulsing DC; an AC generator (alternator) uses slip rings to deliver sinusoidal output. The induced emf depends on the magnetic field strength, number of turns, coil area, and rotational speed: ε = NBAω sin(ωt).

Transformers are the quiet workhorses of the electrical grid. An iron core links two coils. Alternating current in the primary creates alternating flux in the core, which induces emf in the secondary. Faraday's law gives ε_p/N_p = ε_s/N_s = dΦ/dt — so V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p. Energy conservation (minus small losses) means I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s. Real transformers have losses: copper losses (I²R in windings), eddy currents (minimised by laminating the core), and hysteresis (energy lost in each magnetisation cycle of the iron).

Measuring instruments: a moving-coil galvanometer — the heart of analogue ammeters and voltmeters — uses the same torque-on-a-coil principle as a motor, restrained by a spring so the deflection is proportional to current. An ammeter is a galvanometer with a low-resistance shunt in parallel (most current bypasses the sensitive coil). A voltmeter is a galvanometer with a high resistance in series (limiting current draw from the circuit being measured). Digital multimeters use analogue-to-digital converters instead, but the principle of not disturbing the circuit remains: ammeters go in series (low resistance), voltmeters in parallel (high resistance).

faqs.q: What is back emf in a motor?
faqs.a: As a motor's coil spins in the magnetic field, the changing flux induces a voltage (back emf) that opposes the applied voltage. The net voltage driving current is V_applied − V_back. At startup, back emf is zero and current is high. At speed, back emf limits the current.

faqs.q: Why must a voltmeter have high resistance?
faqs.a: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component being measured. If it had low resistance, significant current would flow through the voltmeter, altering the circuit's behaviour. High resistance (ideally infinite) ensures the voltmeter draws negligible current and measures the true potential difference.

faqs.q: How does a transformer change voltage without moving parts?
faqs.a: Alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic flux in the iron core. This changing flux links the secondary coil and, by Faraday's law, induces an emf. The ratio of secondary to primary voltage equals the ratio of their turn counts. No electrical connection exists between primary and secondary — energy transfers purely through the magnetic field.

subject: physics
metaDescription: A beginner-friendly introduction to forces and motion: what is a force, balanced vs unbalanced, speed, acceleration, and simple Newton's laws. Free course.
summary: If you're new to physics, start here. This page explains what forces are, how they affect motion, and why objects speed up, slow down, or change direction. No calculus, no vectors beyond simple arrows — just the core ideas of balanced and unbalanced forces, speed, acceleration, and Newton's first and second laws explained with everyday examples.
bodyHtml:
A force is simply a push or a pull. When you kick a ball, the wind pushes a sail, or gravity pulls you toward the ground, a force is acting. Forces are measured in newtons (N). One newton is roughly the weight of a small apple — the force of gravity on a 100 g mass.

Forces can be balanced or unbalanced. Balanced forces (equal and opposite on the same object) cancel out — the object either stays still or keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line. A book sitting on a table has gravity pulling down and the table pushing up, equal and opposite — the forces are balanced. A car cruising at constant speed on a flat road has the engine's forward force balanced by air resistance and friction.

When forces are unbalanced, the object accelerates — it speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. Acceleration isn't just getting faster; braking (slowing down) and turning (changing direction) are also acceleration in physics. Newton's second law captures this: acceleration = net force ÷ mass. For the same force, a lighter object accelerates more. For the same mass, a bigger force gives more acceleration.

Common forces you'll meet: Weight always pulls straight down (mg, where g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth). Normal reaction pushes straight out from a surface — it's what stops you falling through the floor. Friction opposes sliding and always acts along the surface. Tension pulls along a rope or string. Air resistance (drag) opposes motion through air and grows with speed — this is why falling objects reach a terminal speed where drag balances weight.

Speed is how fast something moves (metres per second, m/s). Velocity is speed with a direction. Acceleration is how quickly speed changes (m/s per second, or m/s²). If a car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 seconds, its acceleration is 5 m/s². If it brakes from 20 m/s to 0 in 2 seconds, its acceleration is −10 m/s² (deceleration).

faqs.q: What is a force in simple terms?
faqs.a: A force is a push or a pull on an object. It can make an object start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction. Gravity, friction, tension in a rope, and the push of wind are all forces. Forces are measured in newtons (N).

faqs.q: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
faqs.a: Speed tells you how fast something is moving — 10 m/s. Velocity tells you how fast AND in what direction — 10 m/s north. In everyday language we use them interchangeably, but in physics, changing direction means velocity changes even if speed stays the same.

faqs.q: Why do heavier objects need more force to accelerate?
faqs.a: Mass is a measure of inertia — resistance to changes in motion. A heavier object has more inertia, so the same force produces less acceleration. This is Newton's second law: a = F/m. Push a shopping cart and a car with the same force — the cart accelerates much more because it has less mass.

subject: physics
metaDescription: A beginner's guide to energy: kinetic, potential, work, power, and conservation of energy explained simply with everyday examples. Free course.
summary: Energy is what makes things happen. It comes in different forms — motion, height, heat, electricity — and it never disappears, only changes form. This beginner-friendly page explains kinetic and potential energy, work, power, and why conservation of energy is the most useful shortcut in all of physics. No advanced maths, just clear ideas.
bodyHtml:
Energy is the ability to do work — to make something move, heat up, or change. It's measured in joules (J). One joule is roughly the energy needed to lift a small apple one metre against gravity. Energy is a scalar — it has size but no direction, unlike force or velocity.

Energy comes in many forms that can convert into each other. Kinetic energy (KE) is the energy of motion. A moving car, a flying cricket ball, a running person all have kinetic energy. It depends on mass and speed: KE = ½mv². If you double the speed, kinetic energy quadruples — which is why high-speed crashes are so much worse than low-speed ones.

Gravitational potential energy (GPE) is stored energy due to height: GPE = mgh. Lift something against gravity and you're storing energy that can be released by letting it fall. A roller coaster at the top of a hill has maximum GPE; at the bottom, all that energy has become kinetic — the car is moving its fastest. Hydroelectric dams use this same conversion: water stored high flows down through turbines, turning GPE into electrical energy.

The big idea: energy is conserved. It's never created or destroyed, only transformed from one type to another. In a pendulum, energy swaps back and forth between kinetic (at the bottom) and potential (at the extremes). In a light bulb, electrical energy becomes light and heat — none disappears, though some becomes less useful (heat is harder to harness than electricity).

Work is how forces transfer energy: work = force × distance (in the direction of the force). When you push a box across the floor, you do work. Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: power = energy ÷ time, measured in watts (W). One watt is one joule per second. A 60 W bulb uses 60 joules every second. An Olympic weightlifter might produce 3000 W for a fraction of a second.

faqs.q: Can energy be destroyed?
faqs.a: No. Energy can change form — kinetic to thermal, chemical to electrical — but the total amount in a closed system always stays the same. If it seems like energy has disappeared, it has probably become heat, which spreads out and becomes harder to notice but is still there.

faqs.q: What is the difference between energy and power?
faqs.a: Energy is the total amount (joules). Power is how fast energy is used or transferred (watts = joules per second). A battery stores energy; a motor's power rating tells you how fast it can use that energy. A small battery can power a bright bulb — but only for a very short time.

faqs.q: Why does a pendulum eventually stop swinging?
faqs.a: Friction and air resistance gradually convert the pendulum's mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) into thermal energy — the air and the pivot warm up very slightly. Energy is still conserved, but it leaves the pendulum and spreads into the surroundings where it's no longer useful for swinging.

subject: physics
metaDescription: Learn the basics of electricity: charge, current, voltage, resistance, Ohm's law, and simple circuits — explained for beginners. Free interactive course.
summary: Electricity powers the modern world, and the core ideas are simpler than they seem. This page explains electric charge, current (the flow of charge), voltage (the push), and resistance (the opposition). With just these three concepts and Ohm's law, you can understand how every basic circuit works. Intended for beginners — no prior physics needed.
bodyHtml:
Electricity starts with charge, a fundamental property of matter. Electrons carry negative charge; protons carry positive charge. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. Charge is measured in coulombs (C), and the charge on one electron is −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C — unbelievably tiny. A single AA battery pushes about 10²² electrons through a torch bulb before it goes flat.

Current is the flow of charge. It's measured in amperes (A, or 'amps'): 1 A = 1 coulomb per second flowing past a point. In metal wires, the moving charges are electrons. But by convention, current direction is defined as the flow of positive charge — so in a wire, the electrons flow one way and the 'conventional current' points the other way. This historical oddity doesn't matter for circuit analysis as long as you're consistent.

Voltage (potential difference) is the energy per unit charge — the 'push' that drives current around a circuit. It's measured in volts (V): 1 V = 1 joule per coulomb. A 9 V battery gives each coulomb of charge 9 J of energy. Think of voltage as the height of a waterfall and current as the flow rate of water — a taller drop (higher voltage) can drive more flow.

Resistance is the opposition to current flow, measured in ohms (Ω). A thin, long wire has more resistance than a thick, short one. Resistance turns electrical energy into heat — this is how a filament bulb glows and an electric heater warms a room. The key equation is Ohm's law: V = IR. Voltage equals current times resistance. For a given voltage, more resistance means less current. For a given resistance, more voltage means more current.

In a series circuit, components are connected end to end — the same current flows through everything, but the voltage is shared. In a parallel circuit, components are connected side by side — each gets the full voltage, but the current is shared. Household wiring uses parallel connections so every appliance gets full mains voltage regardless of what else is plugged in.

faqs.q: What is the difference between current and voltage?
faqs.a: Current (amps) is the flow rate of charge — how many coulombs pass per second. Voltage (volts) is the energy per unit of charge — the push that makes the charge flow. Using water as an analogy: voltage is the water pressure, current is the flow rate through the pipe.

faqs.q: What does Ohm's law tell me?
faqs.a: V = IR: the voltage across a resistor equals the current through it multiplied by its resistance. If you know any two of V, I, and R, you can find the third. Ohm's law only applies to 'ohmic' materials (metals at constant temperature) — many electronic components don't follow it.

faqs.q: Why is household wiring in parallel, not series?
faqs.a: In series, if one appliance fails or is turned off, the circuit is broken and everything stops. In parallel, each appliance has its own path to the supply — you can switch them on and off independently. Also, parallel ensures each gets the full voltage; in series, voltage would be divided.

subject: physics
metaDescription: Learn the basics of waves: transverse vs longitudinal, wavelength, frequency, amplitude, sound waves, light waves, and the wave equation. Free course.
summary: Waves carry energy from one place to another without carrying matter. They're how we hear, see, and communicate. This beginner-friendly page covers the two types of waves (transverse and longitudinal), the vocabulary (wavelength, frequency, amplitude, speed), how sound and light are both waves, and why the wave equation v = fλ ties it all together.
bodyHtml:
A wave is a disturbance that travels, carrying energy but not matter. Drop a stone in a pond: the ripples spread outward, but the water itself mostly bobs up and down — it doesn't travel outward with the ripples. All waves share this property.

Waves come in two types. Transverse waves: the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction the wave travels. Light, radio waves, and ripples on a string are transverse. Longitudinal waves: the oscillation is along the direction of travel — regions of compression and rarefaction. Sound in air is longitudinal; the air molecules vibrate back and forth in the same direction the sound travels.

Every wave is described by a few key numbers. Amplitude (A) is the maximum displacement from rest — for sound, this determines loudness; for light, brightness. Wavelength (λ, lambda) is the distance between two successive crests (or compressions). Frequency (f) is the number of complete oscillations per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Period (T) is the time for one complete oscillation: T = 1/f. Wave speed (v) is how fast the disturbance travels.

These quantities are linked by the wave equation: v = fλ. Speed = frequency × wavelength. For a given medium, speed is fixed — so if frequency increases, wavelength must decrease to keep the product constant. This is why a high-pitched sound has a shorter wavelength than a low-pitched sound travelling in the same air.

Sound waves are longitudinal pressure variations in a medium (air, water, solids). Humans hear from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sound travels at about 343 m/s in air, 1,480 m/s in water, and about 5,000 m/s in steel. Light waves are transverse electromagnetic waves — they need no medium and travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum. The frequency of visible light ranges from about 4 × 10¹⁴ Hz (red) to 8 × 10¹⁴ Hz (violet). Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays are all the same thing — electromagnetic waves — differing only in frequency (and therefore wavelength).

faqs.q: What is the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves?
faqs.a: In transverse waves, the vibration is perpendicular to the direction of travel (like a rope shaken up and down). In longitudinal waves, the vibration is along the direction of travel (like a spring pushed and pulled). Light is transverse; sound in air is longitudinal.

faqs.q: What is the wave equation?
faqs.a: v = fλ — wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength. It applies to ALL waves. If you know any two of speed, frequency, and wavelength, you can find the third. For a given medium, speed is constant, so higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

faqs.q: Can sound travel through space?
faqs.a: No. Sound is a mechanical wave — it needs a medium (air, water, solid) to propagate because it works by particles bumping into each other. In the vacuum of space, there are no particles to transmit the vibration. That's why space is silent, and why astronauts communicate by radio (electromagnetic waves, which don't need a medium).

seoTitle: Heat & Matter Basics for Beginners — Qubix
metaDescription: Learn the basics of heat and matter: temperature, states of matter, thermal expansion, specific heat capacity, and changes of state. Free beginner course.
summary: Heat is energy in transit, and it changes matter in predictable ways. This beginner-friendly page explains temperature vs heat, the three common states of matter and how heat drives transitions between them, why materials expand when heated, and what specific heat capacity tells you. Everyday concepts made precise, with a free interactive course to practise.
bodyHtml:
Temperature and heat are not the same thing. Temperature (measured in kelvin, K, or degrees Celsius, °C) tells you the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance — how vigorously they're jiggling. Heat (measured in joules, J) is the total thermal energy transferred from a hotter object to a cooler one. A spark has a very high temperature but contains very little heat. A bathtub of warm water has a moderate temperature but contains far more heat than the spark.

Matter exists in three common states: solid, liquid, and gas. In solids, particles are tightly packed in fixed positions — they vibrate but don't move around. In liquids, particles are still close but can slide past each other — the substance has fixed volume but no fixed shape. In gases, particles fly around independently and fill whatever container they're in — neither fixed shape nor volume. Changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing) happen at specific temperatures for a given substance — water melts/freezes at 0 °C and boils/condenses at 100 °C (at standard pressure). During a change of state, temperature stays constant even as heat is added or removed — the energy goes into breaking or forming bonds between particles, not increasing their kinetic energy.

Most materials expand when heated because particles vibrate more vigorously and occupy slightly more space. This is why bridges have expansion joints, railway tracks have gaps, and a tight jar lid loosens under hot water (the metal lid expands more than the glass). The expansion is ΔL = αL₀ΔT, where α is the coefficient of linear expansion — different for every material.

Specific heat capacity (c) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K). Water has an unusually high specific heat capacity (about 4,200 J/kg·°C) — this is why coastal climates are milder than inland ones (the ocean absorbs and releases heat slowly) and why water is an excellent coolant. Metals have low specific heat capacities — they heat up and cool down quickly. The heat energy equation: Q = mcΔT — energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.

faqs.q: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
faqs.a: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles — how hot something feels. Heat is the total thermal energy transferred due to a temperature difference. A bucket of warm water has much more heat than a red-hot spark, even though the spark has a far higher temperature.

faqs.q: Why does temperature stay constant during melting or boiling?
faqs.a: The energy being added goes into breaking the bonds between particles (solid → liquid or liquid → gas), not into increasing their kinetic energy. Once all the bonds are broken and the change of state is complete, the temperature starts rising again.

faqs.q: Why does water have such a high specific heat capacity?
faqs.a: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules means a lot of energy goes into increasing molecular vibration and rotation, not just translation. This makes water an excellent thermal buffer — it heats up and cools down slowly, which has enormous implications for climate, weather, and life.

subject: physics
metaDescription: A beginner's guide to optics: how light travels, reflection, refraction, how mirrors and lenses form images, and how the eye sees. Free course.
summary: Light is how we see everything. This beginner-friendly page explains what light is, how it travels in straight lines, bounces off mirrors, bends through lenses, and forms the images our eyes detect. No complex equations — just the core ideas of reflection, refraction, and how lenses help us see near and far.
bodyHtml:
Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines (in a uniform medium) at an incredible speed — 300,000,000 metres per second in vacuum. Nothing travels faster. When light hits an object, some of it bounces off into our eyes, and that's how we see. The ray model — thinking of light as narrow beams travelling in straight lines — is the simplest way to understand mirrors, lenses, and shadows.

Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. The rule is simple: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the 'normal' — an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface at the point of contact. A mirror has a perfectly smooth surface, so all rays from the same incident direction bounce in the same reflected direction — you see a clear image. A rough surface (like paper or a wall) scatters light in all directions — you see the surface but no reflected image. Both obey the same law; the difference is surface smoothness.

Refraction is light bending when it passes from one transparent medium to another — air to water, air to glass. The bending happens because light changes speed. It slows down in denser media (water, glass) and bends toward the normal. It speeds up going into a rarer medium and bends away from the normal. This is why a straw in a glass of water looks bent at the surface, and why a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.

Lenses use refraction to bend light in useful ways. A convex lens (thicker in the middle) converges light — it brings parallel rays together at a focal point. This is the type used in magnifying glasses, cameras, and your eye. A concave lens (thinner in the middle) diverges light — it spreads parallel rays outward. Your eye contains a convex lens that focuses light onto the retina at the back. If the eyeball is too long or the lens too strong, distant objects focus in front of the retina — that's short-sightedness, corrected by diverging (concave) spectacle lenses. If the eyeball is too short, near objects focus behind the retina — long-sightedness, corrected by converging (convex) lenses.

Colour: white light is a mixture of all visible colours. A prism splits white light into a spectrum because each colour refracts by a slightly different amount — violet bends most, red least. The colour of an object is the light it reflects: a red apple reflects red wavelengths and absorbs the others.

faqs.q: Why does a straw look bent in a glass of water?
faqs.a: Light from the underwater part of the straw changes speed and bends (refracts) as it leaves the water and enters the air. Your brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it interprets the bent rays as the straw being in a position it's not really in.

faqs.q: How does a magnifying glass work?
faqs.a: A convex lens bends light rays from an object so they converge at your eye. When the object is placed inside the lens's focal length, the lens creates a virtual image that is larger and farther away than the actual object — your eye sees a magnified view.

faqs.q: What causes a rainbow?
faqs.a: Sunlight enters water droplets in the air, refracts (bends) as it enters, reflects off the back inside surface of the droplet, and refracts again as it exits. Different colours bend by slightly different amounts, so the white sunlight spreads into a circular spectrum. You see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you and rain is ahead.

seoTitle: Getting Infinitely Close — Limits Explained — Qubix
metaDescription: Understand limits in calculus: what it means to approach a value infinitely closely, one-sided limits, limits at infinity, and the epsilon-delta definition. Free course.
h1: Getting infinitely close — the idea of a limit
summary: The limit is the foundation of calculus. It captures the idea of approaching a value arbitrarily closely without necessarily reaching it. This page explains limits intuitively (a moving point closing in), then formally (ε–δ), with examples of limits that exist, limits that don't, and limits that reveal removable discontinuities.
bodyHtml:
A limit describes the value a function approaches as its input approaches some point. Write lim_{x→a} f(x) = L to mean: we can make f(x) as close to L as we like by taking x sufficiently close (but not equal) to a. The function doesn't need to be defined at x = a — the limit is about the trend, not the exact point.

Consider f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1). At x = 1 this is 0/0, undefined. But factor the numerator: f(x) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x − 1). For every x ≠ 1, this simplifies to x + 1. So as x approaches 1 from either side, f(x) approaches 2. The limit exists and equals 2, even though f(1) doesn't exist. This is a removable discontinuity — the hole can be 'plugged' by defining f(1) = 2.

One-sided limits: lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) is the limit as x approaches from the left (smaller values); lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) is from the right. The two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal. For the floor function ⌊x⌋, as x approaches 1 from below, ⌊x⌋ → 0; from above, ⌊x⌋ → 1. The one-sided limits differ, so lim_{x→1} ⌊x⌋ does not exist.

Limits at infinity describe end behaviour: lim_{x→∞} f(x) = L means f(x) settles toward L as x grows arbitrarily large. For f(x) = 1/x, lim_{x→∞} 1/x = 0 and lim_{x→0⁺} 1/x = ∞. Horizontal asymptotes are limits at infinity; vertical asymptotes are infinite limits at finite x-values.

The formal ε–δ definition: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means for every ε > 0 (no matter how small) there exists δ > 0 such that if 0 < |x − a| < δ, then |f(x) − L| < ε. This is the rigorous foundation that underpins all of calculus — differentiation and integration both rest on limits.

faqs.q: What is a limit in simple terms?
faqs.a: A limit is the value a function gets closer and closer to as the input approaches some number. It describes the trend, not necessarily the actual value at that point. The function might not even be defined at the point — the limit only cares about what happens nearby.

faqs.q: When does a limit not exist?
faqs.a: A limit fails to exist when the left-side and right-side limits are different (jump discontinuity), when the function grows without bound (infinite limit), or when the function oscillates too wildly to settle on any single value (like sin(1/x) near x = 0).

faqs.q: What is the epsilon-delta definition for?
faqs.a: It provides a rigorous, testable meaning for 'arbitrarily close.' Instead of vague intuition, it says: tell me how close you want f(x) to be to L (ε), and I can tell you how close x must be to a (δ) to guarantee it. This eliminates hand-waving from proofs.

seoTitle: Turning Points & Area Under Curves — Qubix
metaDescription: Learn how calculus finds maxima, minima, and the area under curves: differentiation for turning points, integration for area. Free interactive maths course.
summary: Calculus answers two fundamental questions: where does a function reach its highest or lowest point, and how much area sits under a curve? Differentiation finds turning points by locating where the slope is zero. Integration computes area by summing infinitely many thin slices. This page shows both operations and why they're inverses of each other.
bodyHtml:
Turning points (stationary points) are where a function's derivative equals zero — the tangent is horizontal. To find them: differentiate f(x) to get f'(x), solve f'(x) = 0 for x, then classify each using the second derivative. If f''(x) > 0, it's a local minimum (U-shaped). If f''(x) < 0, it's a local maximum (∩-shaped). If f''(x) = 0, it could be a point of inflection — check whether the derivative changes sign.

For f(x) = x³ − 3x, f'(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1). Setting f'(x) = 0 gives x = ±1. At x = −1, f''(−1) = −6 < 0 → local maximum. At x = 1, f''(1) = 6 > 0 → local minimum. The function rises from −∞, peaks at x = −1, dips to a trough at x = 1, then rises again.

Second derivative test: compute f''(x) at each stationary point. Positive → minimum. Negative → maximum. Zero → inconclusive (examine sign of f' on either side). This is faster than the first derivative sign test and directly reveals concavity.

Area under a curve from x = a to x = b is the definite integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx. If f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b], this is the actual geometric area. If f(x) dips below zero, the integral gives signed area — regions below the axis contribute negatively. To get total geometric area, split the interval at the roots and take absolute values.

The simplest case: the area under f(x) = x² from 0 to 2 is ∫_0² x² dx = [x³/3]_0² = 8/3 ≈ 2.67. Compare with a triangle of base 2 and height 4 (area 4) — the parabola sits below the straight line, so its area is smaller.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links differentiation and integration as inverse operations. If F'(x) = f(x), then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). The integral of a rate of change gives the total change — which is why these two seemingly unrelated problems (slopes and areas) are solved by the same two tools.

faqs.q: How do I find the maximum or minimum of a function?
faqs.a: Differentiate to get f'(x). Solve f'(x) = 0 — these are your stationary points. Use the second derivative: f''(x) > 0 means minimum, f''(x) < 0 means maximum. If f''(x) = 0, check the sign of f' on either side.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a definite and indefinite integral?
faqs.a: An indefinite integral ∫ f(x) dx gives a family of functions (antiderivatives) — it includes '+ C'. A definite integral ∫_a^b f(x) dx gives a single number — the signed area between the curve and the x-axis from a to b.

faqs.q: Why are differentiation and integration inverse operations?
faqs.a: Differentiation gives the rate of change; integration accumulates change. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus proves they're inverses: if you integrate the derivative of a function, you get the original function back (up to a constant). This is why both rely on the limit concept.

metaDescription: Master coordinate geometry: points, lines, circles, parabolas, distance formula, slope, equations of loci, and conic sections. Free interactive maths course.
summary: Coordinate geometry (or analytic geometry) uses algebra to describe shapes. Every point is a pair of numbers (x, y); every line is a linear equation; every circle is a quadratic. This page covers the distance formula, slope, equations of lines and circles, and how to translate geometric problems into algebraic ones and back.
bodyHtml:
Coordinate geometry bridges algebra and geometry. A point becomes a pair (x, y). The distance between two points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²] — Pythagoras' theorem on the coordinate plane. The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

The slope (gradient) of a line through two points is m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Slope measures steepness: m = 0 is horizontal, m = 1 is 45°, negative slopes go downhill. Two lines are parallel if they have the same slope. Two lines are perpendicular if their slopes multiply to −1: m₁m₂ = −1. The angle between two lines is tanθ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.

A line can be written in several forms. Slope–intercept: y = mx + c, where m is slope and c is the y-intercept. Point–slope: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), useful when you know one point and the slope. General form: Ax + By + C = 0, which handles vertical lines (B = 0). The distance from a point (x₀, y₀) to the line Ax + By + C = 0 is |Ax₀ + By₀ + C|/√(A² + B²).

A circle with centre (h, k) and radius r has equation (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Expanding gives the general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, with centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c). The equation of a tangent to a circle at a given point uses the fact that the tangent is perpendicular to the radius.

More advanced: parabolas have the defining property that each point is equidistant from a focus (a point) and a directrix (a line). The standard parabola y² = 4ax has focus (a, 0) and directrix x = −a. Similarly, ellipses (sum of distances to two foci is constant) and hyperbolas (difference of distances to two foci is constant) make up the conic sections, all describable by second-degree equations in x and y.

faqs.q: How do I find the distance between two points?
faqs.a: Use the distance formula: d = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]. This is Pythagoras' theorem applied to the horizontal and vertical differences between the points.

faqs.q: What does the slope of a line tell me?
faqs.a: Slope (m) measures steepness and direction. Positive m means the line rises left to right; negative means it falls. m = 0 is horizontal; a vertical line has undefined slope. The numerical value is the rise (y-change) divided by the run (x-change).

faqs.q: How do I find the equation of a circle?
faqs.a: If you know the centre (h, k) and radius r, use (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². If the equation is in expanded form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, the centre is (−g, −f) and radius is √(g² + f² − c). For this to be a real circle, g² + f² − c must be positive.

h1: Arithmetic foundations — the building blocks of maths
summary: Before algebra, before calculus, there's arithmetic — the rules for working with numbers. This page covers the number system (natural, integer, rational, real), fractions and decimals, percentages, factors and multiples, and the order of operations. These are the tools every other branch of mathematics is built on.
bodyHtml:
Numbers come in nested families. Natural numbers ℕ: 1, 2, 3, … (the counting numbers). Integers ℤ: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … (natural numbers plus zero and negatives). Rational numbers ℚ: any number expressible as a fraction a/b where a and b are integers and b ≠ 0. Their decimal expansions either terminate (¼ = 0.25) or repeat (⅓ = 0.333…). Irrational numbers: numbers that cannot be expressed as fractions — their decimals go on forever without repeating (π, √2, e). Together, rationals and irrationals make the real numbers ℝ, a continuous number line with no gaps.

Fractions: a/b means a parts of size 1/b each. Equivalent fractions scale numerator and denominator by the same factor: ½ = 2/4 = 3/6. To add or subtract, find a common denominator. To multiply, multiply tops and bottoms separately: (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/(bd). To divide, multiply by the reciprocal: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c) = ad/(bc).

Decimals are fractions with denominator a power of 10. Converting a fraction to a decimal: divide numerator by denominator. Converting a terminating decimal to a fraction: write it over the appropriate power of 10 and simplify. For repeating decimals, a clever algebraic trick works — let x = 0.272727…, then 100x = 27.2727…, subtract to get 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11.

Percentages: 'per cent' means per hundred. 25% = 25/100 = ¼. To find a percentage of a quantity, multiply by the percentage divided by 100. A 15% increase means multiply by 1.15; a 20% decrease means multiply by 0.80. Percentage change = (new − old)/|old| × 100%.

Order of operations: PEMDAS/BODMAS — Parentheses/Brackets, Exponents/Orders, Multiplication and Division (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right). Factors divide a number exactly; multiples are the number multiplied by integers. The greatest common divisor (GCD) and least common multiple (LCM) are the largest shared factor and smallest shared multiple of two numbers, respectively.

faqs.q: What is a rational number?
faqs.a: A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction a/b where a and b are integers and b ≠ 0. Its decimal expansion either terminates or repeats. Examples: ½, −3, 0.75, 0.333… Irrational numbers like π or √2 cannot be expressed this way.

faqs.q: Why do we need a common denominator to add fractions?
faqs.a: Fractions with different denominators represent parts of different-sized wholes. ½ + ⅓ doesn't make sense directly — is it 'half a thing plus a third of a thing'? Converting both to sixths (3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6) gives them a shared unit, making addition straightforward.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a factor and a multiple?
faqs.a: A factor divides a number exactly (3 is a factor of 12). A multiple is the number multiplied by an integer (12 is a multiple of 3). Factors are ≤ the number; multiples are ≥ the number (for positive integers). 12's factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. 3's multiples: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, …

h1: Algebra foundations — the language of mathematics
summary: Algebra replaces numbers with letters so you can express general relationships. Instead of saying '3 + 4 = 4 + 3,' algebra says 'a + b = b + a for all numbers a and b.' This page covers variables, algebraic expressions, solving linear and quadratic equations, factorisation, and the laws that govern how algebraic expressions are manipulated.
bodyHtml:
Algebra uses variables (letters) to stand for numbers that might be unknown or might vary. An expression like 3x² − 2x + 5 combines variables and constants with operations. An equation asserts that two expressions are equal: 3x + 2 = 11. Solving it means finding the value(s) of x that make it true.

Solving a linear equation: isolate x by doing the same operation to both sides. 3x + 2 = 11 → subtract 2: 3x = 9 → divide by 3: x = 3. Every step preserves equality. For equations with variables on both sides, collect like terms first: 5x − 3 = 2x + 9 → 3x = 12 → x = 4.

Quadratic equations have an x² term: ax² + bx + c = 0. Three main methods: factorisation (x² − 5x + 6 = 0 → (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 → x = 2 or 3), completing the square (x² + 6x + 5 = 0 → (x + 3)² − 4 = 0 → x = −1 or −5), and the quadratic formula: x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/(2a). The discriminant D = b² − 4ac tells you the nature of the roots: D > 0 gives two real roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, D < 0 gives two complex roots.

Factorisation is the reverse of expansion. Recognise patterns: difference of squares a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); perfect square a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²; sum/difference of cubes. For a quadratic ax² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, then split the middle term and factor by grouping.

Laws of indices (exponents): a^m × a^n = a^{m+n}; a^m ÷ a^n = a^{m−n}; (a^m)^n = a^{mn}; a^0 = 1 (for a ≠ 0); a^{−n} = 1/a^n; a^{1/n} = ⁿ√a. These laws are not arbitrary — they're forced by the requirement that exponent rules stay consistent when you extend from positive integers to zero, negatives, and fractions.

faqs.q: What is the quadratic formula?
faqs.a: x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/(2a) gives the solutions to ax² + bx + c = 0. It's derived by completing the square on the general quadratic. The ± means there are generally two solutions — one with + and one with − before the square root.

faqs.q: Why is a⁰ = 1?
faqs.a: It follows from the index law a^m ÷ a^n = a^{m−n}. If m = n, then a^m ÷ a^m = 1, and a^{m−m} = a⁰. For consistency, a⁰ must equal 1 (for a ≠ 0). It's not an arbitrary definition — it's forced by the pattern.

faqs.q: How do I factorise a quadratic when a ≠ 1?
faqs.a: For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to ac and sum to b. Split the middle term bx into those two parts. Then factor by grouping the first two and last two terms. Example: 2x² + 7x + 3 → ac = 6, need sum 7 → 6 and 1 → 2x² + 6x + x + 3 → 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) → (2x + 1)(x + 3).

summary: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers that represents a linear transformation — a way of stretching, rotating, or shearing space. This page covers the basics of matrix arithmetic, how to multiply matrices (and why the order matters), determinants, inverses, solving systems of linear equations, and what eigenvalues tell you about a transformation.
bodyHtml:
A matrix is a grid of numbers with m rows and n columns. An m × n matrix represents a linear map from ℝⁿ to ℝᵐ: it takes an input vector, multiplies and adds its components in a specific pattern, and outputs a new vector. The identity matrix I (1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere) leaves every vector unchanged: Ix = x.

Matrix multiplication is not element-by-element. For AB to be defined, the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. The (i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. This rule is not arbitrary — it's exactly what you get when you compose two linear transformations. Crucially, AB ≠ BA in general. Rotation then reflection is not the same as reflection then rotation.

The determinant of a square matrix, det(A) or |A|, is a single number that tells you how the transformation scales area (in 2D) or volume (in 3D). For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], det = ad − bc. A determinant of zero means the transformation collapses space to a lower dimension — it's not invertible. A negative determinant means orientation is flipped (a reflection is involved). The determinant of a product is the product of determinants: det(AB) = det(A) det(B).

The inverse A⁻¹ undoes the transformation: A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I. A matrix is invertible iff its determinant is non-zero. For a 2 × 2, A⁻¹ = (1/det) [[d, −b], [−c, a]]. Solving a linear system Ax = b multiplies both sides by A⁻¹: x = A⁻¹b. This is the matrix version of dividing both sides of an equation.

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors: for a square matrix A, if Ax = λx for some non-zero vector x and scalar λ, then x is an eigenvector and λ is its eigenvalue. An eigenvector is a direction that A simply stretches or compresses, without rotating. The eigenvalues are roots of the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI) = 0. Eigenvalues reveal the essential nature of a transformation — whether it's a rotation (complex eigenvalues), a projection (zero eigenvalue), or a scaling.

faqs.q: Why does matrix multiplication order matter?
faqs.a: Matrix multiplication corresponds to composing transformations. Doing transformation B then A (giving AB) is generally different from A then B (giving BA). Rotating then reflecting produces a different result than reflecting then rotating. Only for special pairs do matrices commute.

faqs.q: What does a zero determinant mean?
faqs.a: It means the transformation collapses space — at least one dimension is squashed to zero. The matrix has no inverse because information is lost and can't be recovered. Geometrically, a 2 × 2 matrix with det = 0 maps the entire plane onto a line or a point.

faqs.q: What are eigenvalues useful for?
faqs.a: Eigenvalues tell you the fundamental nature of a linear transformation: the directions that are purely stretched (eigenvectors) and by how much (eigenvalues). They're used in stability analysis, Google's PageRank, principal component analysis in data science, vibration analysis in engineering, and quantum mechanics.

h1: Exponents and logarithms — growth and its inverse
summary: Exponents describe repeated multiplication; logarithms are their inverse, answering 'what power?' This page covers the laws of exponents, the definition and rules of logarithms, the natural logarithm and e, exponential growth and decay models, and how to solve equations where the unknown is in the exponent.
bodyHtml:
Exponents (or indices) are shorthand for repeated multiplication: a^n means a multiplied by itself n times. But the definition extends: a⁰ = 1, a^{−n} = 1/a^n, a^{1/n} = ⁿ√a, a^{m/n} = (ⁿ√a)^m. The laws are consistent across all these cases: a^m · a^n = a^{m+n}, (a^m)^n = a^{mn}, a^m/a^n = a^{m−n}, (ab)^n = a^n b^n.

Logarithms answer: to what power must the base be raised to get a given number? If b^x = y, then log_b(y) = x. A logarithm is an exponent. The log base 10 of 1000 is 3 because 10³ = 1000. The log base 2 of 32 is 5 because 2⁵ = 32. Logs turn multiplication into addition: log_b(xy) = log_b(x) + log_b(y). They turn division into subtraction: log_b(x/y) = log_b(x) − log_b(y). They bring exponents down: log_b(x^n) = n log_b(x).

The natural logarithm ln(x) = log_e(x) uses base e ≈ 2.71828…, a number that emerges naturally from continuous growth. If something grows at a rate proportional to its current size — compound interest, bacterial growth, radioactive decay — the number e appears. The function e^x is its own derivative, making it uniquely important in calculus. ln(x) is the inverse of e^x: ln(e^x) = x and e^{ln x} = x (for x > 0).

Exponential growth follows y = A e^{kt}. If k > 0, the quantity doubles in fixed time intervals (doubling time = ln(2)/k). Exponential decay has k < 0: y = A e^{−kt}. Radioactive decay follows this pattern — the half-life is ln(2)/k. These models appear in population biology, finance, pharmacology (drug clearance), and physics (capacitor discharge, Newton's law of cooling).

Solving equations: for a^x = b, take logs of both sides: x ln(a) = ln(b), so x = ln(b)/ln(a). For log equations, use the definition to rewrite in exponential form: log₂(x + 1) = 3 → x + 1 = 2³ = 8 → x = 7. Always check that solutions keep the argument of the logarithm positive — the domain of log_b(x) is x > 0.

faqs.q: What is a logarithm in simple terms?
faqs.a: A logarithm is the opposite of an exponent. If 2³ = 8, then log₂(8) = 3 — it asks '2 to what power gives 8?' Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, which made them essential for computation before calculators and still matters for solving exponential equations.

faqs.q: Why is e (2.718…) so important?
faqs.a: e is the unique number such that the function e^x equals its own derivative. It describes continuous, proportional growth — the limit of (1 + 1/n)^n as n → ∞. It appears whenever a quantity's rate of change is proportional to its current value: compound interest, population growth, radioactive decay.

faqs.q: How is exponential growth different from linear growth?
faqs.a: Linear growth adds a constant amount each period (y = mx + c). Exponential growth multiplies by a constant factor each period (y = A·b^x). A linear salary gets the same raise each year; exponential investing grows by percentage, so gains compound. Exponential growth eventually outruns any linear growth, no matter how steep.

summary: Trigonometry starts with right-angled triangles but extends to circles, waves, and periodic phenomena of every kind. This page covers the three basic ratios (sine, cosine, tangent), the unit circle as the natural home of trig functions, radians versus degrees, key identities, and how sine and cosine describe everything from pendulums to AC electricity.
bodyHtml:
In a right-angled triangle, the three trigonometric ratios are defined relative to one of the acute angles θ: sinθ = opposite/hypotenuse, cosθ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tanθ = opposite/adjacent = sinθ/cosθ. For a 3–4–5 triangle, if θ is opposite the side of length 3, sinθ = 3/5 = 0.6, cosθ = 4/5 = 0.8, tanθ = 3/4 = 0.75. These ratios depend only on the angle, not the triangle's size — similar triangles have the same angles and therefore the same trig ratios.

The unit circle (radius 1, centre at the origin) extends trigonometry beyond acute angles. A point on the circle at angle θ (measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis) has coordinates (cosθ, sinθ). This definition works for any angle: cos 120° = −½, sin 270° = −1. It also reveals the fundamental identity: cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 (Pythagoras on the unit circle).

Radians are the natural angle measure: 2π radians = 360°. One radian is the angle that makes the arc length equal to the radius. In calculus, the derivative of sin x is cos x only when x is in radians — using degrees introduces an awkward factor of π/180. Radians make the mathematics clean. Common angles: π/6 = 30°, π/4 = 45°, π/3 = 60°, π/2 = 90°, π = 180°.

Key identities: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1; 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ; 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ. The addition formulae: sin(A + B) = sinA cosB + cosA sinB; cos(A + B) = cosA cosB − sinA sinB. Double-angle: sin 2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ; cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = 2 cos²θ − 1 = 1 − 2 sin²θ. The sine and cosine rules extend trigonometry to non-right triangles: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C (sine rule); a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A (cosine rule).

The graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x are smooth waves of period 2π, amplitude 1, shifted by π/2 relative to each other. y = tan x has period π and vertical asymptotes at x = π/2 + nπ. By adjusting amplitude (A), frequency (k), and phase shift (φ), y = A sin(kx + φ) models any sinusoidal wave — sound, tides, AC voltage, pendulum motion.

faqs.q: What is the unit circle and why is it useful?
faqs.a: The unit circle (radius 1 centred at the origin) defines sinθ and cosθ for all angles, not just acute ones. Any point on the circle has coordinates (cosθ, sinθ). It makes the graphs, identities, and periodic nature of trig functions geometrically obvious.

faqs.q: Why use radians instead of degrees?
faqs.a: Radians measure angle by arc length, so they're dimensionless and natural for calculus. The derivative of sin x is cos x only when x is in radians. Also, many formulas (arc length = rθ, sector area = ½r²θ) are simpler in radians without conversion factors.

faqs.q: What is the sine rule and when do I use it?
faqs.a: The sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it when you know two angles and one side (find another side), or two sides and a non-included angle (find another angle — but beware the ambiguous case where two different triangles are possible).

h1: Problem-solving heuristics — the art of finding a way in
summary: Mathematics isn't just about knowing formulas — it's about knowing what to do when you don't know what to do. This page covers general problem-solving strategies (heuristics): drawing a clear diagram, working backwards from the answer, solving a simpler version first, looking for patterns, checking extreme cases, and the crucial habit of asking 'does this answer make sense?'
bodyHtml:
George Pólya's How to Solve It (1945) distilled problem-solving into four stages: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, and look back. Most people skip the first and last steps, diving into algebra before they know what's being asked and never checking whether their answer is plausible.

Understand the problem: restate it in your own words. Identify what's given and what's unknown. Draw a diagram and label everything you know. If the problem involves a physical situation, sketch it. Can you guess a rough answer before calculating? If the answer is supposed to be a length, is it roughly 1 m or 1000 m?

Devise a plan using heuristics. Solve a simpler version: replace 100 with 5 and see what happens. Work backwards: start from the desired result and ask what must be true just before. Find a pattern: compute the first few cases and look for regularity. Draw a diagram: many problems that seem abstract become obvious when visualised. Check extreme cases: what happens when a variable goes to zero or infinity? Consider special cases: if a statement is true for all triangles, it must be true for an equilateral one — test it there first.

Carry out the plan: work step by step, checking each line. Don't rush. One algebraic slip can cascade. Write clearly — future you, re-reading, should be able to follow the logic without reconstructing it.

Look back: does the answer satisfy the original conditions? Plug it back in. Is the magnitude plausible? Can you get the same result a different way? Can you use this method for other problems? This reflective step is where deeper learning happens — you're not just solving one problem, you're building a mental toolkit.

An example: find the sum of integers from 1 to 100. The brute-force approach is tedious. But pair 1 + 100 = 101, 2 + 99 = 101, …, 50 pairs of 101 each — total 5050. The heuristic is symmetry + pairing. Gauss supposedly discovered this at age 7. The general formula for 1 + 2 + … + n is n(n + 1)/2.

faqs.q: What are heuristics in maths problem-solving?
faqs.a: Heuristics are general strategies that often help, unlike algorithms which guarantee a solution. Examples: draw a diagram, solve a simpler case, look for patterns, work backwards, check extreme cases. They're mental tools you try when no formula obviously applies.

faqs.q: What should I do when I'm stuck on a problem?
faqs.a: Step back and clarify what you're really being asked. Try a simpler version. Draw a diagram. Talk through the problem aloud. Check if you're using all the given information. Take a short break — your subconscious continues working. If still stuck, identify exactly where the block is and tackle that sub-problem.

faqs.q: Why does working backwards help?
faqs.a: Working backwards starts from the desired result and asks what conditions would produce it, then what conditions produce those, and so on until you reach the given information. It reverses the logical flow and often reveals a path that isn't obvious going forward. It's especially useful in geometry proofs and equation-solving.
