subject: maths
metaDescription: Extend your problem-solving toolkit: invariants, parity arguments, pigeonhole principle, proof by contradiction, and mathematical induction. Free course.
summary: Beyond drawing diagrams and working backwards lie more powerful heuristics. Invariants — quantities that don't change — crack problems that seem to have too many moving parts. Parity arguments reduce possibilities by a factor of two. The pigeonhole principle guarantees that in any large enough set, some collision must occur. Contradiction and induction provide ironclad proofs.
bodyHtml:
Invariants: in many problems, something stays the same through all the changes allowed by the rules. A classic puzzle: a chessboard with two opposite corners removed — can you cover it with 31 dominoes, each covering two adjacent squares? The invariant is colour: each domino covers one black and one white square. The mutilated board has 32 of one colour and 30 of the other — impossible. Finding the right invariant is an art, but when you find it, the problem collapses.

Parity (even/odd) is the simplest invariant. The sum of two odd numbers is even; the product of two odd numbers is odd. Parity arguments eliminate half the possibilities instantly. If a closed loop of 2025 light switches is toggled so each switch changes state exactly once, can all end up on? Each toggling flips parity — tracking parity often solves problems about reachable states.

The pigeonhole principle: if n items are placed into m boxes and n > m, at least one box contains multiple items. Simple, but powerful. In any group of 367 people, at least two share a birthday (there are only 366 possible birthdays). Among any five points inside a square of side 2, two are at most √2 apart (divide the square into four 1 × 1 quadrants — by the pigeonhole principle, two points share a quadrant).

Proof by contradiction: assume the opposite of what you want to prove, and logically derive an impossibility. Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes: assume there are finitely many. Multiply them all together, add 1 — this number is not divisible by any of them, so it's either a new prime or has a prime factor not in the list. Contradiction.

Mathematical induction: prove a statement for n = 1 (base case), then prove that if it holds for n = k, it holds for n = k + 1 (inductive step). Together, these prove the statement for all natural numbers — like knocking over an infinite row of dominoes. Induction proves formulas for sums, divisibility properties, and inequalities that hold for all n.

faqs.q: What is an invariant?
faqs.a: An invariant is a property that stays the same even as other things change. In the mutilated chessboard problem, the difference between the number of black and white squares is an invariant. Finding the right invariant is often the key to proving that some state can or cannot be reached.

faqs.q: How does proof by induction work?
faqs.a: Two steps: (1) prove the statement is true for n = 1 (or the smallest applicable value). (2) assume it's true for n = k and prove it must then be true for n = k + 1. If both hold, the statement is true for all positive integers. Think of it as 'if it works for 1, it works for 2; if it works for 2, it works for 3…'

faqs.q: What is the pigeonhole principle?
faqs.a: If you put more pigeons than holes, at least one hole gets multiple pigeons. Formally: if n items go into m categories and n > m, at least one category contains at least two items. It's a simple counting observation that yields surprisingly strong guarantees in combinatorics and number theory.

metaDescription: Apply vectors and matrices to solve problems: linear systems, transformations, geometry proofs, eigenvalues in action. Free interactive maths course.
summary: Vectors and matrices aren't just notation — they're problem-solving tools. This page shows how to use vectors to prove geometric theorems elegantly, how matrices solve systems of linear equations systematically, and how eigenvalue decomposition reveals the deep structure of linear transformations. The focus is on using these tools to crack problems, not just define them.
bodyHtml:
Vectors shine in geometry proofs. To prove the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other: let the vertices be O, A, B, and A + B (parallelogram law). The midpoint of diagonal OB is (0 + A + B)/2 = (A + B)/2. The midpoint of diagonal from A to B is (A + B)/2 — the same point. Four lines of vector algebra replace a page of classical geometry.

For collinearity and concurrency, vectors provide clean tests. Points A, B, C are collinear if AB is a scalar multiple of AC — i.e., the vectors are parallel. The centroid of a triangle is the average of its vertices: G = (A + B + C)/3. Since G lies on the segment from any vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side (in ratio 2:1), you can prove concurrency of medians in a few lines.

Solving linear systems with matrices: write the system as Ax = b. If det(A) ≠ 0, the unique solution is x = A⁻¹b. But computing inverses by hand for large systems is impractical — instead use Gaussian elimination: transform the augmented matrix [A|b] to row-echelon form using three operations (swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero constant, add a multiple of one row to another). Back-substitution then yields the solution. This algorithm is what computers run when you ask them to solve linear systems.

When det(A) = 0, the system has either no solution (inconsistent — the equations contradict) or infinitely many solutions (the rows are dependent — less information than variables). The rank of a matrix — the number of linearly independent rows — tells you which. Rank < number of unknowns means infinite solutions; an inconsistency means the augmented matrix has higher rank than A alone.

Eigenvalue problems: many problems in physics and engineering reduce to Av = λv. The allowed λ values (eigenvalues) determine the natural frequencies of a vibrating system, the principal axes of stress in a material, or the stable population distribution in an ecological model. Diagonalisation — writing A = PDP⁻¹ where D is diagonal — decouples the system into independent one-dimensional problems, each scaled by its eigenvalue.

faqs.q: How do vectors simplify geometry proofs?
faqs.a: Vectors let you express geometric relationships algebraically. Instead of drawing auxiliary lines and chasing angles, you write points as position vectors, sides as difference vectors, and conditions (parallel, perpendicular, midpoint) as algebraic equations. The algebra does the heavy lifting.

faqs.q: What is Gaussian elimination?
faqs.a: It's a systematic algorithm for solving linear systems. You write the coefficients as an augmented matrix, then use row operations to create zeros below the diagonal (forward elimination), then solve from the bottom up (back-substitution). It works for any size system and is the basis of most numerical linear algebra.

faqs.q: What does it mean to diagonalise a matrix?
faqs.a: Diagonalisation expresses a matrix A as PDP⁻¹ where D is diagonal (only the main diagonal has non-zero entries). The diagonal entries are the eigenvalues. This decouples the system — instead of all variables interacting, each new coordinate evolves independently, making the dynamics easy to analyse.

h1: Lockhart's algebra — foundations through a mathematician's eyes
summary: Paul Lockhart's approach to algebra treats it not as a set of rules to memorise, but as the study of successive number systems and the operations they permit. This page follows that spirit: from natural numbers through integers, rationals, reals, and complexes, each expansion driven by the desire to solve equations the previous system couldn't handle.
bodyHtml:
Algebra, in Lockhart's view, is not about solving for x — it's about understanding the behaviour of operations in different number systems. Each number system is defined by what equations you can solve within it.

Natural numbers ℕ let you solve x + 3 = 7 (x = 4), but not x + 7 = 3. To subtract any number from any number, you need integers ℤ, which include negatives. Now x + 7 = 3 yields x = −4. But integers can't solve 3x = 7 — you need rational numbers ℚ (fractions). Now 3x = 7 gives x = 7/3.

Rationals fail at x² = 2. The Greeks proved √2 is irrational — it can't be expressed as a fraction. To solve x² = 2, you need real numbers ℝ, which fill the gaps between rationals. Reals solve x² = a for any a ≥ 0, but they fail at x² = −1. No real number squares to give a negative. So you extend again to complex numbers ℂ, defining i = √(−1). Now every polynomial equation has a solution (the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra).

This pattern — extending the number system to solve previously unsolvable equations — is the grand narrative of algebra. At each step, you gain new operations (subtraction, division, roots) but must check that the old rules still hold. Does a + b = b + a work for complex numbers? Yes. Does a(b + c) = ab + ac? Yes. The field axioms (commutativity, associativity, distributivity, identity, inverses) are preserved through each extension.

Lockhart emphasises algebra as creative play: take a pattern you notice — say, (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² — and ask what it means geometrically (area of a square of side a + b). Ask what happens when you extend it: (a + b + c)², or (a + b)³. Generate your own conjectures, test them with numbers, and only then try to prove them. Mathematics isn't received wisdom; it's a playground you're invited into.

faqs.q: Why do we need complex numbers?
faqs.a: Complex numbers, built from i = √(−1), are the algebraically complete number system — every polynomial equation has a solution in ℂ. They're not just abstract; they're essential in electrical engineering (AC circuit analysis), quantum mechanics (wave functions), and signal processing (Fourier transforms).

faqs.q: What does Lockhart mean by algebra as art?
faqs.a: Lockhart argues that school algebra is taught as a dead set of rules when it should be taught as a creative, exploratory activity — like music or painting. You play with patterns, make conjectures, test them, and find elegant explanations. The process of mathematical discovery, not the answer, is the point.

faqs.q: Why can't √2 be written as a fraction?
faqs.a: The classic proof by contradiction: assume √2 = p/q in lowest terms. Then 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q², meaning p² is even, so p is even. Write p = 2k, then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k², meaning q is also even. But p and q can't both be even if the fraction is in lowest terms — contradiction. Therefore √2 is irrational.

metaDescription: Explore symmetry in algebra: polynomial roots, factorisation, the fundamental theorem, and the deep link between symmetry and solvability. Free course.
summary: Why are some polynomial equations solvable by radicals and others not? The answer, discovered by Galois, is symmetry. This page explores the connection between a polynomial's roots and the symmetries of the equation they satisfy. From the quadratic formula to the insolvability of the quintic, symmetry is the organising principle.
bodyHtml:
A polynomial equation like x² − 5x + 6 = 0 has roots x = 2 and x = 3. The coefficients (1, −5, 6) are symmetric functions of the roots: the sum of the roots is 5, the product is 6. This is true for any quadratic: x² − (sum of roots)x + (product of roots) = 0. The coefficients are symmetric polynomials in the roots — swapping the roots doesn't change them.

For a cubic x³ + ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots r, s, t: a = −(r + s + t), b = rs + rt + st, c = −rst. These are the elementary symmetric polynomials — every symmetric polynomial in the roots can be expressed in terms of the coefficients. This is the bridge between roots and the coefficients you're given.

Vieta's formulas generalise this to any degree. For a_n x^n + a_{n−1} x^{n−1} + … + a_0 = 0 with roots r₁, …, r_n: the sum of roots = −a_{n−1}/a_n, the sum of products of pairs = a_{n−2}/a_n, alternating signs, and the product of all roots = (−1)^n a_0/a_n.

Galois theory asks: which permutations of the roots preserve all algebraic relationships among them? The set of such permutations forms a group — the Galois group of the polynomial. If this group has a particular structure (called solvability), the roots can be expressed using radicals (square roots, cube roots, etc.). The quadratic formula exists because the Galois group of a quadratic is always the 2-element group, which is trivially solvable. For cubics and quartics, the groups are more complex but still solvable.

The dramatic result: the general quintic (degree 5) has Galois group S₅, the symmetric group on 5 elements, which is not solvable. Therefore there is no general quintic formula in radicals — not because no one has found it, but because it does not and cannot exist. This is one of the most beautiful results in mathematics, connecting the ancient problem of solving equations to the abstract algebra of groups and symmetry.

faqs.q: What are Vieta's formulas?
faqs.a: They relate a polynomial's coefficients to sums and products of its roots. For x² + px + q = 0, the sum of roots is −p and the product is q. They're useful for finding one root given another, checking your work, and constructing polynomials with specified roots.

faqs.q: Why is there no formula for quintic equations?
faqs.a: Galois theory proves that the symmetric group S₅ (the permutations of 5 roots) is not a solvable group. Since the Galois group of the general quintic is S₅, no formula using only radicals (square roots, cube roots, etc.) can express its roots. This is a proven impossibility, not an open problem.

faqs.q: What is a symmetric polynomial?
faqs.a: A polynomial whose value stays the same when you swap any of the variables. For example, x² + y² is symmetric; x² − y² is not (swapping gives y² − x² = −(x² − y²)). The coefficients of a polynomial are always symmetric functions of its roots — this is the fundamental link between coefficients and roots.

h1: Calculus — differentiation, the mathematics of change
summary: Differentiation measures how fast something changes, at an exact instant. From the slope of a curve to the velocity of a particle, the derivative captures instantaneous rate of change. This page builds the derivative from first principles (limits), covers the rules that make differentiation practical (product, quotient, chain), and shows how derivatives solve real problems.
bodyHtml:
The derivative of a function f at a point x is the limit of the difference quotient: f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. Geometrically, this is the slope of the tangent line — the limit of secant line slopes as the two points converge. For f(x) = x²: f'(x) = lim_{h→0} [(x + h)² − x²]/h = lim_{h→0} (2xh + h²)/h = lim_{h→0} (2x + h) = 2x.

The derivative is a function in its own right. f'(x) tells you the instantaneous rate of change of f at every x where the limit exists. The notations f'(x), dy/dx, and d/dx[f(x)] all mean the same thing. Leibniz's dy/dx notation is especially useful because it reminds you that a derivative is a ratio of infinitesimal changes and makes the chain rule visually obvious.

Rules that make differentiation practical: power rule: d/dx[x^n] = nx^{n−1}. Sum rule: (f + g)' = f' + g'. Product rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg'. Quotient rule: (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g². The chain rule: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) · g'(x) — differentiate the outer function evaluated at the inner, then multiply by the derivative of the inner. In Leibniz notation: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx), which makes the rule almost obvious.

Implicit differentiation: when y is defined implicitly as a function of x (like x² + y² = 25, a circle), differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y as a function of x and using the chain rule on y terms. For the circle: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y. This gives the slope at any point without solving for y explicitly.

Applications: optimisation (find maxima/minima by setting f'(x) = 0), related rates (how fast does the water level drop when the tank drains?), curve sketching (f' > 0 means increasing; f' < 0 means decreasing; f'' tells concavity), and linear approximation: f(x + Δx) ≈ f(x) + f'(x)Δx — the tangent line as a local linear model.

faqs.q: What is a derivative in simple terms?
faqs.a: A derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change — how fast something is changing right now. On a graph, it's the slope of the tangent line at a point. If f(t) is position, f'(t) is velocity. If f(x) is cost, f'(x) is marginal cost — the cost of producing one more unit.

faqs.q: How does the chain rule work?
faqs.a: When you have a function inside another function — like sin(x²) — the chain rule says: differentiate the outer function (sin → cos), keeping the inner the same, then multiply by the derivative of the inner. d/dx[sin(x²)] = cos(x²) · 2x. It's the most-used differentiation rule.

faqs.q: What is implicit differentiation and when do I need it?
faqs.a: Use it when you can't (or don't want to) solve for y explicitly as a function of x. Differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to x, treating y as a function of x. Every time you differentiate a y term, multiply by dy/dx (chain rule). Then solve for dy/dx.

h1: Calculus — integration, the mathematics of accumulation
summary: Integration is the inverse of differentiation and the mathematics of accumulation — adding up infinitely many infinitesimal pieces to get a whole. This page covers indefinite and definite integrals, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the Riemann sum definition, and the main techniques: substitution, integration by parts, and partial fractions.
bodyHtml:
Integration answers two kinds of questions. Indefinite integration: given a derivative, what was the original function? ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, where F'(x) = f(x). Definite integration: what is the signed area between the curve y = f(x) and the x-axis from a to b? ∫_a^b f(x) dx.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links these: if F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). This is astonishing — computing an area (which involves a limit of sums) reduces to evaluating an antiderivative at two points. It's the reason calculus works as a practical tool.

Why is the antiderivative the area function? Define A(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt — the area under f from a to x. Then A'(x) = f(x). The rate at which area accumulates at x is just the height of the curve at x. So the area function is an antiderivative. The FTC is the formal proof of this intuition.

Techniques: u-substitution reverses the chain rule. For ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx, let u = x², du = 2x dx, giving ∫ cos u du = sin u + C = sin(x²) + C. The art is spotting an inner function whose derivative appears (up to a constant factor) in the integrand. Integration by parts reverses the product rule: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. It's powerful for products where one factor simplifies when differentiated (like x e^x) or where the integrand is a single function you know how to differentiate but not integrate (like ln x).

Partial fractions decompose rational functions (one polynomial divided by another) into simpler fractions you can integrate with logs and arctangents. For ∫ (3x + 5)/(x² − 1) dx, factor the denominator and write as A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 1). Solve for A and B, then integrate each term separately.

Applications: area between curves (∫ [f(x) − g(x)] dx), volumes of revolution (disc method: V = π∫ [f(x)]² dx; shell method: V = 2π∫ x f(x) dx), arc length, average value of a function over an interval, and work done by a varying force.

faqs.q: What is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus?
faqs.a: It states that differentiation and integration are inverse operations. Part 1: if F'(x) = f(x), then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a). Part 2: the function A(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt is an antiderivative of f. It connects the two big ideas of calculus — rates of change and accumulated quantity.

faqs.q: When should I use u-substitution?
faqs.a: Look for a function and (roughly) its derivative in the integrand. If you see something like ∫ x e^{x²} dx, let u = x², du = 2x dx, and the integral becomes ∫ (1/2) e^u du. The inner function's derivative (2x) is present (x), so substitution works. It's the most common integration technique.

faqs.q: What does '+ C' mean in an indefinite integral?
faqs.a: The derivative of a constant is zero, so if F(x) is an antiderivative of f(x), so is F(x) + C for any constant C. The '+ C' acknowledges that indefinite integration gives a family of functions, not a single one. The constant is determined by an initial condition — knowing the function's value at a specific point.

metaDescription: Journey inside the atom: protons, neutrons, electrons, atomic number, mass number, isotopes, and how the subatomic particles were discovered. Free course.
h1: Into the atom — the building blocks of matter
summary: Everything you can touch is made of atoms, and atoms are mostly empty space. A dense nucleus of protons and neutrons sits at the centre, with electrons forming a diffuse cloud around it. This page explains what's inside the atom, how we know, and what atomic number and mass number tell you about any element.
bodyHtml:
An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains its chemical identity. Its diameter is about 10⁻¹⁰ m — a hundred million would fit across your fingernail. The nucleus occupies only about 1/10,000 of this diameter but contains over 99.9% of the mass. The rest is the electron cloud — a region where electrons are likely to be found, not a fixed orbit.

The nucleus contains two types of particles. Protons carry a positive charge (+1) and have a mass of approximately 1 atomic mass unit (u). Neutrons carry no charge and have roughly the same mass. The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons — it defines the element. Carbon always has 6 protons; change that and it's not carbon. The mass number (A) is the total number of protons plus neutrons. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons; carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons — same element, different isotope.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same Z) with different numbers of neutrons (different A). They have nearly identical chemical properties because chemistry is governed by electrons, which depend on Z, not A. Some isotopes are stable; others are radioactive and decay over time, which is the basis of carbon dating.

Electrons carry a negative charge (−1) and have negligible mass (about 1/1836 of a proton). In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. Electrons don't orbit like planets — they occupy orbitals, three-dimensional regions where the probability of finding the electron is high. The arrangement of electrons into shells and subshells determines how the atom bonds and reacts.

The historical path to this model: Thomson discovered the electron (1897) and proposed the 'plum pudding' model. Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1909) showed the atom was mostly empty space with a dense, positively charged nucleus. Bohr (1913) proposed fixed energy levels for electrons. The modern quantum mechanical model replaced fixed orbits with probability clouds (orbitals), resolving the contradictions of the Bohr model.

faqs.q: What is an isotope?
faqs.a: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. For example, carbon-12 (6 protons, 6 neutrons) and carbon-14 (6 protons, 8 neutrons) are both carbon, but carbon-14 is radioactive.

faqs.q: Why don't electrons fall into the nucleus?
faqs.a: In classical physics they would — an accelerating charge radiates energy and should spiral in. Quantum mechanics resolves this: electrons exist in stationary states (orbitals) with fixed energies. They can't lose energy continuously; they jump between discrete levels. The lowest-energy orbital has a non-zero distance from the nucleus — the electron can't get closer without violating the uncertainty principle.

faqs.q: How did Rutherford discover the nucleus?
faqs.a: He fired alpha particles (helium nuclei) at a thin gold foil. Most passed through with little deflection, but about 1 in 8,000 bounced back. Rutherford said it was 'as if you fired a 15-inch shell at tissue paper and it came back and hit you.' The only explanation: the atom's positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

seoTitle: Atomic Structure: Orbitals & Electron Config — Qubix
metaDescription: Master atomic structure: quantum numbers, electron configuration, orbitals (s, p, d, f), the Aufbau principle, and periodic trends. Free chemistry course.
h1: Atomic structure — orbitals and electron configuration
summary: Where exactly are the electrons in an atom? Quantum mechanics answers with orbitals — probability clouds with specific shapes and energies. This page covers the four quantum numbers, the shapes of s, p, and d orbitals, how electrons fill them (Aufbau principle, Hund's rule, Pauli exclusion), and how electron configuration explains the periodic table's structure.
bodyHtml:
Electrons in atoms are described by four quantum numbers. The principal quantum number n (1, 2, 3, …) determines the shell and roughly the energy. The azimuthal quantum number l (0 to n − 1) determines the subshell shape: l = 0 is s (spherical), l = 1 is p (dumbbell), l = 2 is d (cloverleaf), l = 3 is f (complex). The magnetic quantum number m_l (−l to +l) determines the orbital's orientation in space. The spin quantum number m_s (+½ or −½) is the electron's intrinsic angular momentum.

Orbitals are not orbits. An s orbital is a sphere around the nucleus; the electron could be anywhere inside, with highest probability at a certain radius. Three p orbitals (p_x, p_y, p_z) are shaped like dumbbells along each axis. Five d orbitals have more complex shapes. Orbitals represent regions where there's a high (typically 90%) probability of finding the electron. They are solutions to the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom and serve as the building blocks for multi-electron atoms.

Electrons fill orbitals following three rules. Aufbau principle: fill lowest-energy orbitals first (1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p …). Pauli exclusion principle: each orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins. Hund's rule: when filling degenerate orbitals (like the three p orbitals), place one electron in each with parallel spins before pairing up. This minimises electron–electron repulsion.

Electron configuration is written compactly: oxygen (Z = 8) is 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. The periodic table's shape emerges directly from orbital filling. The s-block (groups 1–2) fills s orbitals; the p-block (groups 13–18) fills p orbitals; the d-block (transition metals) fills d orbitals; the f-block (lanthanides and actinides) fills f orbitals. Periodic trends — atomic radius decreasing across a period, ionisation energy increasing, electronegativity increasing — are all consequences of increasing nuclear charge pulling electrons closer while shielding from inner shells partially offsets the pull.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an orbit and an orbital?
faqs.a: An orbit (Bohr model) is a fixed circular path like a planet's orbit — the electron has a definite position and velocity. An orbital (quantum model) is a probability cloud — a region where the electron is likely to be found. The orbital picture is more accurate; electrons don't follow fixed paths.

faqs.q: Why does 4s fill before 3d?
faqs.a: The energy ordering is 4s < 3d for potassium and calcium because the 4s electron penetrates closer to the nucleus on average, experiencing less shielding. However, once 3d starts filling, it drops below 4s in energy — which is why transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d when forming ions.

faqs.q: What explains the periodic trend in atomic radius?
faqs.a: Across a period (left to right), nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell. The increased pull from the nucleus draws electrons closer, so atomic radius decreases. Down a group, electrons occupy higher shells (larger n), so radius increases despite the larger nuclear charge.

h1: Chemical bonding — why atoms stick together
summary: Atoms bond because bonded states have lower energy than separated atoms. The type of bond — ionic, covalent, or metallic — depends on how the electrons are shared or transferred. This page covers Lewis structures, electronegativity, bond polarity, VSEPR theory for molecular shape, and the weaker intermolecular forces that hold liquids and solids together.
bodyHtml:
Chemical bonds form because electrons rearrange to give atoms more stable configurations — typically a full outer shell (octet). Ionic bonding: electrons transfer from one atom to another. Sodium (Na, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹) loses one electron to become Na⁺ with a neon-like configuration. Chlorine (Cl, …3s² 3p⁵) gains one to become Cl⁻ with an argon-like configuration. The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions forms the ionic bond. Ionic compounds form crystal lattices, not discrete molecules.

Covalent bonding: electrons are shared between atoms. In H₂, each hydrogen contributes one electron to a shared pair that both nuclei attract. The shared pair occupies a molecular orbital that concentrates electron density between the nuclei, screening their positive charges from each other. Lewis structures represent covalent bonds as lines (shared pairs) and non-bonding electrons as dots. Carbon dioxide is O=C=O — two double bonds, each with two shared pairs.

Electronegativity measures an atom's pull on shared electrons (Pauling scale: F = 4.0, highest; Cs ≈ 0.7, lowest). When atoms with different electronegativities bond, the sharing is unequal — a polar covalent bond. In HCl, chlorine pulls electron density toward itself, giving H a partial positive charge (δ⁺) and Cl a partial negative charge (δ⁻). If the difference exceeds about 1.7, the bond is considered ionic.

VSEPR theory (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) predicts molecular shape: electron pairs around a central atom repel and arrange to maximise separation. 2 pairs → linear (180°, BeCl₂). 3 pairs → trigonal planar (120°, BF₃). 4 pairs → tetrahedral (109.5°, CH₄). Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles — water (H₂O) has 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs, giving a bent shape with angle ~104.5°.

Metallic bonding: metal atoms pool their outer electrons into a 'sea' of delocalised electrons. The positive metal ions are held in a lattice by attraction to this electron sea. This explains metals' conductivity (electrons move freely), malleability (ions can slide past each other without breaking specific bonds), and lustre (the electron sea interacts with light across a continuous range of energies).

faqs.q: What is the difference between ionic and covalent bonds?
faqs.a: Ionic bonds involve electron transfer — one atom gives up electrons, another gains them, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract. Covalent bonds involve electron sharing — atoms contribute electrons to shared pairs that both nuclei attract. Most real bonds lie on a spectrum between purely ionic and purely covalent.

faqs.q: How does VSEPR theory predict molecular shape?
faqs.a: Count the electron pairs (bonding + lone) around the central atom. These pairs repel and arrange to maximise angular separation. The number of pairs determines the basic geometry (2 → linear, 3 → trigonal planar, 4 → tetrahedral, etc.). Lone pairs take up more space, slightly reducing bond angles.

faqs.q: Why can metals conduct electricity?
faqs.a: In metallic bonding, the outer electrons are delocalised — they belong to the whole lattice, not individual atoms. These mobile electrons can flow in response to an applied electric field, carrying current. The positive ion cores stay in place, so the metal doesn't decompose during conduction.

summary: Chemistry comes alive in reactions — bonds breaking and forming to create new substances. This page covers the major reaction types (synthesis, decomposition, combustion, displacement), how to balance equations and calculate quantities (stoichiometry), and the architecture of organic molecules: functional groups, isomerism, and how molecular shape determines function.
bodyHtml:
Chemical reactions rearrange atoms — no atoms are created or destroyed. A balanced equation respects this conservation: the same number of each type of atom appears on both sides. Stoichiometry uses these balanced ratios to calculate how much product forms from given reactants.

Major reaction types: Synthesis (A + B → AB — combining simpler substances, like 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). Decomposition (AB → A + B — breaking down, like CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ when limestone is heated). Combustion (fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O — hydrocarbons burning, releasing energy). Single displacement (A + BC → AC + B — a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one, like Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu). Double displacement (AB + CD → AD + CB — ions swap partners, often forming a precipitate, like AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃).

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon's ability to form four covalent bonds and catenate (link to itself in chains and rings) creates an enormous diversity of molecules. Functional groups are specific atom groupings that confer characteristic reactivity: alcohols (−OH), carboxylic acids (−COOH), amines (−NH₂), aldehydes and ketones (>C=O), esters (−COOR). A molecule's properties are largely determined by its functional groups.

Isomerism: same molecular formula, different arrangement. Structural isomers have different connectivity — butane and isobutane are both C₄H₁₀ but with different carbon skeletons. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different 3D arrangement. Geometric isomers (cis/trans) differ in the orientation of groups around a double bond. Optical isomers (enantiomers) are non-superimposable mirror images — like left and right hands — with identical physical properties except for how they rotate plane-polarised light. This chirality is crucial in biochemistry: one enantiomer of a drug may be therapeutic, the other toxic.

Molecular architecture directly determines function. The shape of an enzyme's active site matches its substrate. The helical structure of DNA allows information storage and replication. The arrangement of polymer chains determines whether a plastic is rigid or flexible. Chemistry at this level is molecular engineering.

faqs.q: How do I balance a chemical equation?
faqs.a: Count atoms of each element on both sides. Adjust coefficients (numbers in front of formulas) until atom counts match. Never change subscripts — that changes the substance. Start with elements that appear in the fewest compounds, and save hydrogen and oxygen for last. Check your work by recounting.

faqs.q: What is a functional group?
faqs.a: A functional group is a specific arrangement of atoms within a molecule that gives it characteristic chemical behaviour. For example, the −OH group makes a molecule an alcohol — prone to hydrogen bonding, with higher boiling points and specific reactions. Identifying functional groups is the first step in predicting how an organic molecule will react.

faqs.q: What is the difference between structural and stereoisomers?
faqs.a: Structural isomers have the same atoms but bonded in a different order (different connectivity). Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but differ in 3D spatial arrangement. Enantiomers (mirror-image stereoisomers) are a particularly important class — they're chemically identical in achiral environments but behave differently in biological systems.

metaDescription: Master redox reactions, oxidation numbers, electrochemical cells, reaction rates, activation energy, and catalysts. Free interactive chemistry course.
summary: Redox reactions move electrons between species — they power batteries, drive corrosion, and sustain life through respiration. Electrochemistry harnesses these electron transfers to do work. Kinetics explains how fast reactions happen and what energy barriers control the rates. This page connects all three: redox is the 'what,' electrochemistry is the 'how we use it,' and kinetics is the 'how fast.'
bodyHtml:
Redox (reduction–oxidation) reactions involve electron transfer. Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain. (OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.) You can't have one without the other — the electrons lost by one species are gained by another. Oxidation numbers track where electrons 'belong': in a pure element, ON = 0; for monatomic ions, ON equals the charge; oxygen is usually −2; hydrogen is usually +1. If ON increases, the atom is oxidised; if it decreases, it's reduced.

Electrochemical cells convert between chemical and electrical energy. A galvanic (voltaic) cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to generate electricity: zinc and copper in a Daniell cell — Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation at anode) and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction at cathode), producing about 1.1 V. An electrolytic cell uses electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction — like splitting water into H₂ and O₂, or electroplating silver onto jewellery.

The electrochemical series ranks substances by their standard reduction potentials. Metals with more negative potentials (like Zn at −0.76 V) are stronger reducing agents — they're more easily oxidised. Metals with more positive potentials (like Ag at +0.80 V) are weaker reducing agents. The cell potential is E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode; if positive, the reaction is spontaneous.

Chemical kinetics is the study of reaction rates. The rate depends on concentration, temperature, surface area, and catalysts. The rate law rate = k[A]^m[B]^n relates rate to concentrations; the exponents m and n are the reaction orders, determined experimentally, not from the balanced equation. Activation energy (E_a) is the minimum energy reactant molecules must have to react — described by the Arrhenius equation: k = A e^{−E_a/(RT)}. A catalyst lowers E_a without being consumed, providing an alternative pathway. Enzymes are biological catalysts with extraordinary specificity.

faqs.q: How do I assign oxidation numbers?
faqs.a: Rules in order: pure elements = 0. Monatomic ions = their charge. Fluorine is always −1. Oxygen is usually −2 (except in peroxides, −1). Hydrogen is +1 with non-metals, −1 with metals. The sum of oxidation numbers equals the overall charge of the species. Any change indicates redox.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a galvanic and electrolytic cell?
faqs.a: A galvanic cell produces electricity from a spontaneous chemical reaction (ΔG < 0). An electrolytic cell uses external electricity to drive a non-spontaneous reaction (ΔG > 0). In both, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode, but the anode is negative in a galvanic cell and positive in an electrolytic cell.

faqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
faqs.a: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. More molecules have enough energy to overcome this lower barrier, so the fraction of effective collisions increases. The catalyst is regenerated at the end — it participates in the mechanism but is not consumed overall. It does not change the equilibrium position, only the rate at which equilibrium is reached.

h1: A free alternative to Brilliant for learning STEM
summary: If you enjoy Brilliant's approach to conceptual STEM learning but want a free option that works on your phone, Qubix might be what you're looking for. It covers physics, maths, and chemistry as short, swipeable 'boards' — one idea at a time — with interactive quizzes to check your understanding. No paywall, no subscription.
bodyHtml:
Qubix is a free STEM learning app built around a simple idea: swipe across concepts, tap to dig deeper. Each topic is a stack of 'boards' — short, illustrated explainers that take about a minute each. You swipe left and right across ideas, and tap to descend through layers of detail. It's designed for the way people actually use their phones: short sessions, one concept at a time.

Like Brilliant, Qubix focuses on conceptual understanding rather than memorisation. A lesson on Newton's laws doesn't just state F = ma — it walks through what net force means, how to draw free-body diagrams, and why a heavier object resists acceleration more. The boards use diagrams, worked examples, and plain-language explanations.

Where Qubix differs: the content delivery is bite-sized and swipeable — think flashcards meet microlearning. There are 900+ boards covering physics, maths, and chemistry, from basic forces and arithmetic up through calculus, thermodynamics, and reaction kinetics. Each topic contains a curated path through these boards, so you're not wandering through a content library — you follow a sequence designed to build understanding step by step.

Qubix is completely free — no paywall, no premium tier, no subscription. It tracks your progress across six mastery levels for each board, so you know what you've covered and what still needs work. Quizzes at the end of each topic let you test your recall.

Things to be aware of: Qubix is a younger project than Brilliant. The content library is growing but doesn't yet match Brilliant's breadth — there's no computer science or data science content, and the problem-solving depth is still expanding. The interface is mobile-first, so the desktop experience is functional but not optimised. If you're looking for deeply interactive simulations or project-based learning, Qubix may not (yet) be the right fit.

faqs.q: Is Qubix really free?
faqs.a: Yes. Qubix has no paywall, no premium tier, and no subscription. All content — all 900+ boards across physics, maths, and chemistry — is freely accessible. The project is designed to make quality STEM education available to anyone with a phone.

faqs.q: How is Qubix different from Brilliant?
faqs.a: Qubix uses a swipe-and-tap microlearning format — short boards you swipe between, each taking about a minute. Brilliant uses longer interactive lessons with embedded problem-solving. Qubix is more mobile-native and completely free; Brilliant has a broader curriculum and more interactive simulations. They're complementary approaches to the same goal of conceptual STEM understanding.

faqs.q: What subjects does Qubix cover?
faqs.a: Physics (mechanics, electricity, thermodynamics, optics, gravitation, and more), mathematics (arithmetic through calculus, plus matrices, trigonometry, and problem-solving), and chemistry (atomic structure, bonding, reactions, redox, and kinetics). Qubix does not currently cover computer science, data science, or biology.

h1: Apps like Brilliant for learning physics and maths
summary: Several apps now take a concept-first approach to STEM learning, similar to Brilliant. Qubix is one of them — free, mobile-native, and built around bite-sized, swipeable boards that explain one idea at a time in physics, maths, and chemistry. This page compares the landscape so you can find what fits your learning style.
bodyHtml:
The landscape of STEM learning apps has expanded. Brilliant pioneered the interactive, concept-first approach — replacing passive video watching with active problem-solving embedded in the lesson. Other apps have since taken different angles on the same core problem: how do you teach physics, maths, and chemistry in a way that builds genuine understanding, not exam-passing reflexes?

Qubix takes a microlearning approach. Each concept is a 'board' — a short, illustrated screen of explanation that you read in about a minute. Swipe right for the next idea, left to go back, and tap to descend through deeper layers. With 900+ boards arranged into 56 curated topics, you can spend five minutes on your commute learning about torque, or half an hour working through the full thermodynamics path. All content is free. Progress is tracked across six mastery levels per board.

Other notable apps in this space: Khan Academy offers the broadest curriculum (STEM plus humanities) with video lectures and exercises, entirely free. Brilliant focuses on interactive problem-solving with polished visualisations, on a subscription model. Photomath and Symbolab focus on step-by-step problem solving, scanning handwritten equations. Wolfram Alpha is a computational knowledge engine — less a learning tool and more a reference.

What distinguishes Qubix: the swipe-and-tap interaction model is genuinely phone-native, not a desktop interface shrunk to mobile. The content is written in plain, concrete language — definitions and scenarios, not hype. And it's free, with no advertising. The trade-off: Qubix is newer and has a smaller content library than the established players.

If you want deeply interactive simulations and the widest range of subjects, Brilliant or Khan Academy may be better fits. If you want a free, mobile-friendly app for learning physics, maths, and chemistry concepts in short sessions, Qubix is worth trying.

faqs.q: What is the best free alternative to Brilliant?
faqs.a: The best choice depends on your learning style. Khan Academy offers the broadest free curriculum with video lectures. Qubix offers free, bite-sized, swipeable STEM lessons optimised for mobile. Both are genuinely free. Qubix is more mobile-native and focused on short sessions; Khan Academy is more comprehensive but less optimised for quick mobile learning.

faqs.q: Can I learn physics properly from an app?
faqs.a: An app can build strong conceptual understanding — the 'why' behind the formulas — which is the foundation that makes problem-solving make sense. For exam preparation or professional-level depth, you'll likely want to supplement with textbooks and problem sets. An app is excellent for the first pass through a concept, especially if you're time-poor.

faqs.q: Is Qubix suitable for complete beginners?
faqs.a: Yes. Qubix has paths specifically labelled 'the basics' for forces, energy, electricity, and optics. These start from first principles — what a force is, what energy means — with no assumed prior knowledge. More advanced paths cover calculus-based physics and university-level topics.

h1: Learn STEM concepts for free, one idea at a time
summary: You don't need an expensive subscription to learn physics, maths, or chemistry properly. Qubix is a free app that breaks STEM subjects into short, illustrated 'boards' — one concept per minute — with quizzes to check your understanding. 900+ boards across 56 topics, from basic forces to quantum numbers, all free.
bodyHtml:
STEM education has a cost problem. Textbooks are expensive. Tutoring is expensive. Many online platforms put their best content behind paywalls. Qubix takes a different approach: every board, every quiz, every topic is free. The project's goal is to make conceptual STEM learning accessible to anyone with a phone.

The content covers three subjects. Physics spans mechanics (forces, energy, torque, gravitation), electricity and magnetism (circuits, induction, AC), thermodynamics and heat transfer, optics (reflection, refraction, lenses, instruments), oscillations and waves, and applied topics like engineering tools and electrical machines. Mathematics runs from arithmetic and algebra foundations through trigonometry, coordinate geometry, matrices, exponents and logarithms, and calculus (both differentiation and integration), plus dedicated problem-solving heuristics paths. Chemistry covers atomic structure, chemical bonding, molecular architecture, reaction types, and redox with electrochemistry and kinetics.

Each topic is a curated path of boards. A board is a single screen — a short explanation, often with a diagram, that you read in about a minute. Swipe to the next idea. Tap to dig deeper into a particular point. The interaction model keeps you moving forward, and the bite-sized format means you can learn in the gaps of your day — waiting for a bus, during a coffee break, winding down before sleep.

Progress tracking uses six mastery levels per board: unwandered (not yet seen), wandered (glanced), checked (read properly), well_read (studied), recalled (passed quiz), and mastered (passed twice). This granularity lets you see exactly what you've covered and identify gaps, without the pressure of a single pass/fail test hanging over every interaction.

The content is written in a plain, definition-driven style. You'll find concrete examples and mechanism explanations rather than motivational language or marketing hype. The focus is on understanding: why the formula works, not just what it says. If you're curious about how the world works at a physical level — and want to learn it properly, for free — Qubix is built for you.

faqs.q: Is Qubix actually free or does it have hidden costs?
faqs.a: Qubix is genuinely free. There is no premium tier, no subscription, no paywall, and no advertising. The entire content library — 900+ boards, 56 topics, all quizzes — is accessible without paying. The project exists to make STEM education accessible.

faqs.q: How long does it take to complete a topic?
faqs.a: Topics vary in length. A short topic might have 5 boards (about 5 minutes to read through). A long one like Electricity & circuits has 17 boards. The mastery system encourages revisiting — reading once, then returning to quiz and solidify. Most learners spread a topic across several short sessions rather than completing it in one sitting.

faqs.q: Do I need a science background to start?
faqs.a: No. Several paths are explicitly labelled 'the basics' and start from first principles. Forces & motion — the basics, Energy — the basics, Electricity — the basics all assume no prior physics knowledge. As your understanding grows, you can move to the more advanced paths on the same topics.
